#6676. A New Azzedine Alaïa Retrospective Goes Beyond the Bandage Dress

The Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco examines the great couturier’s legacy

The bandage dress. The zipper dress. The perforated leather. The jersey hoods. The peplummed chemises. Azzedine Alaïa’s designs may not look so radical now, but almost 50 years ago, he changed the collective tide of fashion. The bandage dress is perhaps the most pervasive bit of his legacy, and it is emblematic of how the late French-Tunisian designer ushered in a new body-conscious silhouette in the ’80s, one made possible by technological innovations in materials that sculpted without any rigid, waist-cinching structure.

Alaïa’s designs “were completely shocking” to the public at the time, recounts Laura Camerlengo, curator in charge of costume and textile arts at the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. She has spent the past four years developing a new exhibition titled “Azzedine Alaïa: Sculpting Fashion,” the first major U.S. retrospective dedicated to the work of the famed couturier. It opened November 21.

Born in 1935 in Tunis, Alaïa first trained as a sculptor, a background evident in his body of work. In 1956, he decamped to Paris to pursue fashion full-time. After a brief internship at the house of Christian Dior, he worked under Guy Laroche for less than two years before taking on his own private clients, then launching his own atelier in the late ’70s. From there, he built the house we know today. His obsession with construction and material innovation allowed him to both celebrate and liberate the female form. He passed away in late 2017 at the age of 82.

Camerlengo first encountered Alaïa’s work as an assistant on the “Patrick Kelly Runway of Love” exhibition that the Philadelphia Museum of Art organized in 2014. “I was intrigued by how many of the new designers in Paris at this time were being supported by US consumers and retailers,” she says. After ascending to her new position in San Francisco years later, she cold-emailed Olivier Saillard, director of the Azzedine Alaïa Foundation in Paris. He was intrigued, and the two began working together on the exhibition almost immediately.

The exhibition focuses on 80 garments from across Alaïa’s celebrated career, divided over a series of archetypes—the bandage dresses, sculptures and shapes, black and white, silhouettes and suiting, and construction and craftsmanship—to explore how his design aesthetic evolved. Interspersed are designs worn by devotees like Tina Turner, Grace Jones, and Rihanna. One final gallery highlights his personal collections of the work of designers he most admired, like Christian Dior and Charles James.

Ahead, Camerlengo speaks to Bazaar about curating the new exhibition, contextualizing Alaïa’s work in today’s fashion landscape, and his enduring legacy.

The exhibition is not chronological. We look at a series of Alaïa’s archetypes like the bandage dress to explore how his design aesthetic evolved over the course of his career. He often himself said that he didn’t want to conform to seasonal trends; he was more interested in the evolution of his designs. And so the gallery shows a mix of objects dating from the 1980s to his final collection in 2017, and they’re largely grouped by type.

When you come in, you are greeted by Grace Jones, as we say, and the seminal purple hooded bandage dress from the fashion Oscars [a French event held in 1985]. As you move through, you’ll see a selection of the zipper dresses, the chiffon gowns, and other works that tie into some of the other themes. In each space, we mix the time periods. And that was something Alaïa himself often said. [He had a running joke that he didn’t know his own age.] He often said he was “as old as the pharaohs.” Basically, time was a construct for him.

That’s a great word for it. We could think of the popularity of the Japanese fashion designers who obscured women’s bodies with their voluminous styles. We could think of the suiting of the period. The 1970s is this period of workplace equality. Women are wearing suits in the style of masculine dress, but that also means they're obscuring their bodies. And then we can think of pop culture. I always think of Diane Keaton’s Annie Hall in 1977.

Some of the individuals I interviewed for my catalog text who were retailers in San Francisco at the time described Alaïa's designs as being like a whiplash. It was a complete 180 from the styles that they had gotten used to over the past decade, which also includes the rise of T-shirts and jeans for women as a mode of dress.

So here you have these very sexy, very form-fitting clothes. And part of the Alaïa aesthetic, as I see it, is the reclamation of the gaze. Rather than women being passively looked at—usually by men—they are instead commanding their own agency. As you said, it was completely earth-shattering and very shocking at the time.

Azzedine Alaïa was one of the few couturiers who could work completely by the methods of tailoring and by draping, start to finish, from the initial concept to the final product. I did not fully appreciate his tailoring and the suits he constructed beforehand. We have a selection of them in a gallery of the exhibition, and their construction is absolutely incredible. The way they fit the body, the way they uplift and empower women through cloth—again, very antithetical to what we saw in the decades prior in the 1970s. These are very form-fitting, tailored at the waist, but they have soft feminine touches as well that give you this interesting mix of femininity and strength at the same time.

Very important. We talk in the first gallery about how women, speaking generally, were the architects of his life. He learned to sew from his sister, who was working for a seamstress. He was encouraged by a local midwife in Tunisia to go to school at the Institute of Fine Arts. She helped him forge his papers to read 16—he was only 15 at the time. He learned his skills, not in formal training, but from women in Tunisia.

And then his early work was supported by a lot of leading figures of international society, including various Rothschilds, the French performer Arletty, the Swedish American actress Greta Garbo, and that's all before he even started to work formally under his own label in the 1980s. Of course, in the 1980s, he adopts Naomi Campbell, who becomes his protégé. He has close relationships with Grace Jones and Tina Turner. They were hugely important to him. In the exhibition, the clear invisible mounts that we use are actually based on the body of Naomi Campbell.

Probably the Grace Jones bandage dress from the fashion Oscars in 1985. Not only is it the progression of the bandage dress style that he experiments with throughout the course of the 1980s, but it represents a key moment in his career where he receives two very high accolades as part of the fashion Oscars and he’s recognized for his genius.

As far as the designs themselves, I think we would consider the bandage dress, for example, an iconic symbol of late 20th- and 21st-century fashion developed by Azzedine Alaïa, but of course iterated upon extensively. We've seen surges and resurgences in its popularity ever since.

And then as far as the landscape of the broader fashion system, Alaïa was someone who really eschewed seasonal calendars and trends. He was unconcerned with making things for the market. He often wanted to just produce clothes and share them when he felt they were ready. So I think his method of working foreshadows some of the conversations we’re having now about the overproduction of fashion and the overconsumption of fashion, even the detrimental environmental impacts that we see connected to it. He was really a forerunner, in a sense, to question the fashion system.

You can see how he really studied the construction of other garments and then adapted it in his own way in his designs. For example, he admired the work of Charles James, the great American fashion designer who was able to manipulate fabric to achieve weightless volume. And you see in Alaïa's own collections as he continues in his career, he does radial tucks and pleating to also get a certain amount of weightless volume in some of his gowns, very much in the spirit of James.

I hope our visitors appreciate the artistry of his work, first and foremost, and also the importance of handcraftsmanship. We are increasingly in an age of technology, especially with the rise of AI. What he created by his own hand is something that we can really marvel at.

#6674. What GQ Editors Impulse-Bought in November

Every day, your faithful, over-caffeinated GQ Recommends editors cover everything from wardrobe essentials to step by step guides on how to find your office fragrance so that you know exactly what to purchase when you're shopping for your everyday items and big-ticket splurges. But, in-between bouts of menswear proselytizing and shilling for Big Gloop we do a lot of shopping for ourselves. And—while we like to think of ourselves as thoughtful consumers—even we smash that add to cart button on a whim a few times a month. That's why we put together this non-exhaustive list of what GQ Recommends editors impulse-bought this month. Here's everything we tossed in our virtual bags against our better judgement.

Am I the only one deeply intrigued by this jacket's above-the-waist crop, capacious pockets, and just-right collar? Someone please investigate and report back. —Avidan Grossman

I already have a couple of pairs of Oni jeans, which means I don't need any more. That said, I could not help myself when I saw these beauties. While most other jeans use a handful of machines to achieve various kinds of stitches that make the process much faster, the 900HM jeans are made using only a single-needle straight stitch machine, essentially doubling the amount of time it takes to make a single pair. —Gerald Ortiz

Everyone's playing GTA but that doesn't mean I can't reminisce about Red Dead Redemption 2. —Jordan Bowman

No one breaches the defenses of my wallet as swiftly as MarieBelle. Look at it! It's beautiful! And it tastes like autumn! —Mari Herrema

Expanding my man's color palette, one accessory at a time. —Mari Herrema

Full disclosure: I didn't impulse buy this recently. I did, however, impulse buy it roughly five years ago, a spur-of-the-moment decision I pat myself on the back for around this time every fall. —Avidan Grossman

As long as the temperature refuses to sink below an arbitrary, say, 50-ish degrees, this is the only lightweight layer you need. —Avidan Grossman

Just some damn good pants. That's all it takes to hit add to cart, sometimes you just know it when you see it. —Jordan Bowman

Personally, I don't think my dad needs any more socks, but it is a guaranteed home-run of a gift for him. —Mari Herrema

I'm on a personal quest to find the ideal everyday derbys, which has led me here. —Jordan Bowman

If you're the type of sicko who swears by shorts year-round, you could do a lot worse than sticking with these. (Also, like, hire me at your startup or whatever.) —Avidan Grossman

It's that time of the year when my notebooks start to reach their last leaves. So I went for a very pristine, unadorned notebook made by one of the best notebook manufacturers on the market. —Gerald Ortiz

The vintage guy in me was pounding through my chest when I saw these rare pants. I've been on the hunt for a good pair of vintage cargos, and the M-43s have always been on my watch list for their unique pockets and herringbone twill fabric, though the right pair never found their way to me. So when this black overdyed pair was listed on eBay, I knew I'd finally found the one. —Gerald Ortiz

Sometimes I feel like telling my dad that giving his Museum Classic to my Garmin-pilled brother is the silliest thing in the world and that I would actually wear the watch. Other times I remember my wrists are not Man Sized and that I make my own money, too. —Mari Herrema

#6672. Your December Horoscope by Zodiac Sign

We’re wrapping up the year with great momentum going into the new year.

December’s astrology helps you wrap the year up with some forward momentum! At the start of the month, the Sun continues its joyful journey through Sagittarius, putting you in a more adventurous mood and encouraging you to expand your horizons and perspective. It's a great time to get in a debate during a holiday dinner and stand up for what you believe in, but to also practice your active listening skills and remain open to the possibility that you could learn something from someone else. You’re zooming out and thinking more about the world around you and eager to soak up life’s experiences by trying new things and meeting new people.

You’re feeling all-or-nothing when it comes to love once Venus moves into Scorpio on December 4. For the next few weeks, Venus is retracing its steps that it took during the retrograde, so you might finally experience relief or turning points regarding some of your key relationships and contracts. This can help you navigate uncomfortable terrain in your close connections with honesty and vulnerability. You’re feeling funnier than normal once Mercury enters Sagittarius on December 6. When our communication planet moves through jokester Sagittarius, your conversations are a bit more playful but words can also sting from time to time. It’s easier to speak what’s on your mind in the moment and regret it later. You might also have a harder time finding a plan or strategy to reach certain goals, but right now you’re not meant to sort through the details. Focus on the big picture and soaking up new information and experiences instead. If you’re traveling, you might also deal with more snafus, so plan accordingly!

A New Moon in Sagittarius on December 8 helps you reconnect with a source of hope or optimism. Conversations feel expansive and information that you learn might inform your worldview in a new way. This energy is also helpful for reframing the way you speak to yourself and releasing limiting beliefs. You might find yourself eager to book some travel or sign up for a workshop to hone a skill or learn something new. You’re not afraid to set firm boundaries when Saturn stations direct in Aries on December 10. This will bring you back to July 26, the day the retrograde began. Similar themes and topics are resurfacing and asking you to be accountable for your own limitations or to set necessary boundaries with courage.

A few days later, on December 12, Neptune stations direct in Aries, helping you to dissolve your ego. This brings you back to July 7, and puts you in touch with certain topics and conversations that were a focus around then. You might feel more tender and sensitive, or feel a burst of creativity. This can help you channel your own creative energy for a higher purpose or ideal to make a positive impact in the collective. On the same day, Jupiter stations retrograde in Leo, bringing a crisis of faith. You could learn news or experience something that rattles your foundation or makes you question your own belief system. This can put you in a philosophical mood, asking you to reflect on whether you’re living in alignment with your beliefs. There might also be developments regarding teachers and mentors in your life, decisions about going back to school, or turning points regarding some of your goals and dreams.

The Sun enters Capricorn on December 21, marking the Winter Solstice in the Northern Hemisphere and the longest night of the year. From now on, the daylight will slowly begin to increase once again. But first, you must move through winter and preserve your precious energy in the process. This is not the time to overdo it or overextend yourself. It’s time to prune people, patterns, and situations from your life that extinguish your drive and essence instead of replenishing them. A Full Moon in Cancer on December 23, highlights your relationship with the past, primary caregivers, and security. There might be significant developments within your chosen family or perhaps you’re making a decision about where you live. People are in a more sentimental mood and the past can stir up major feelings and reflections. Be gentle with yourself and others.

The month wraps up with Mercury entering Capricorn on December 25, lending you a more structured approach to your ideas and communication style. You might find yourself navigating boundaries more or even find yourself speaking with a little more directness. There’s no need to sugarcoat to keep others comfortable, your time is limited and you’ve got things to do! This energy can be productive, help you problem solve, and stick with habits and plans that build toward your longterm success.

#6671. “Focus on Learning”: Career Lessons With Burberry’s Daniel Lee and Anna Wintour

The morning after Vogue World 2026: Milano, all anyone online wanted to talk about was “the robots”. The moment became a lightning rod for memes, TikTok reactions, and questions about the state of creativity today. It turns out that was sort of the point.

A couple of months after the event, Anna Wintour, chief content officer at Condé Nast and global editorial director of Vogue, invited Burberry’s chief creative officer Daniel Lee to New York for a fireside chat at the Vogue Business Global Summit. Lee also wanted to talk about “the robots.”

A robot walks the runway during Vogue World: Milano 2026.

Of course, the two discussed much more than that, taking turns interviewing each other about Lee’s journey at the British brand during a company-wide turnaround, Wintour’s first job in fashion, the US midterms that happened the day before, and success — spoiler: social media makes it look easy. Ahead of the official announcement, Wintour also teased the Met Costume Institute’s theme for 2027: extraORDINARY.

Anna Wintour: Daniel, good morning. Thank you for coming all the way from London. So Daniel, you chose a very quiet news day here in the US. Have you been following the election news?

Daniel Lee: Yeah, definitely. I was super jet-lagged, so I was watching the news all night.

AW: I have to ask you, how do you think [Senator-elect] James Talarico would look in a Burberry suit?

DL: Well, I’d be happy to see anyone looking great in a Burberry suit.

Anna and Daniel on stage at the Vogue Business Global Summit.

AW: Very diplomatic. I guess you’re a Burberry ambassador. I read that you first thought you wanted to be a designer when your aunt took you to see the windows at Harvey Nichols in Leeds as a boy. I guess the equivalent over here would be Saks. Do you agree?

DL: Yes, I’m afraid that is true. You know, I didn’t fall into fashion by looking through pages of Vogue. That’s probably the story I should start saying. I mean, I grew up in the north of England in an area called Yorkshire, which is very beautiful — it’s in the countryside and very green. It rains a lot.

DL: David Hockney is from my hometown. Also, Christopher Bailey is from the same area [Yorkshire]. The Burberry trench coats are made in that area, so I guess Burberry was somehow ingrained in me since I was born. Clothes were really practical in my childhood. Fashion wasn’t something that was really part of my family or my upbringing. We wore clothes to stay warm and dry.

DL: Very Burberry. As kids, we liked to play outside. We would spend our childhood riding bikes in the rain, in Wellington boots. When Harvey Nichols opened in Leeds, I remember going past that store and seeing these incredible windows, and I guess I realized clothes could be so much more. It was like seeing a fantasyland. I guess that’s when I started to think this maybe could be a career for me.

DL: Eventually, yes. As a child, I think my first instinct was to get out of Yorkshire. As much as I love the countryside, I knew there was more. I was curious.

AW: Well, you did just buy a house there, so you must like it?

DL: You stay connected to your roots. But I think, as a 12-year-old, I went to London for the first time, and I remember seeing the variety of people in the streets, seeing the theater, so many things going on. I really wanted to be part of that culture. I think that’s what initially drew me to London and eventually to art school. I went to [Central] Saint Martins. I did an art foundation year, into fashion qualifications later on.

AW: OK. You’re meant to ask me a question now.

DL: Anna, what was your first job in fashion? And what did you learn from it?

AW: I’m going to talk about the first job that I actually enjoyed in fashion, which was working at Harper’s & Queen (now Harper’s Bazaar UK) in London, where there were two to three people — on a good day — in the fashion department. So I went in there, and I was immediately an editor, even though I had zero experience. I was always so very grateful for that training because there were no budgets. I do remember my boss once giving me maybe £10 or £20 and saying, ‘Anna, go to Morocco or go south. Find a sheikh, find a maharaja, and do a shoot.’ And somehow you did. It was just a different attitude. You had to be so creative and make things out of nothing. Because there were no teams at Harper’s & Queen, I learned how to do everything: you covered the market, you did the shoots, you wrote the captions.

When I came to New York, I went to work at Harper’s Bazaar [US]. I got fired fairly immediately because they told me I would never understand the American market, which is probably true. I then landed on my feet at New York Magazine, which was unbelievable training because I was working in a newsroom with guys like Nick Pileggi and Tom Wolfe — all the great writers of that time. They didn’t give a damn about what I did. They put me next to the bathrooms, so I got to see everybody coming in and out. Because nobody cared about fashion or style, they just left me alone. Eventually, I got a call from Condé Nast. It’s interesting when you talk to young people today how they’re focused on success, and they’re not focused on learning. Without the base, you can't succeed.

I’m meant to ask you a question now. So, congratulations on your very successful show in September. I think it was the first time you collaborated with anyone creatively, and the person that you chose to collaborate with is Celia Birtwell — she’s an 85-year-old legend in textile design, a partner to the great Ossie Clark. Did you have to do much convincing to get her involved? Maybe explain to our audience a little bit more about who she is.

DL: I would say Celia is probably mostly known as Ossie Clark’s collaborator in all those years of incredible dresses and work that I think is on every designer’s moodboard. And she was also very, very close friends with David Hockney and is a subject in many beautiful pieces of his work. We were celebrating 170 years of Burberry this year. We wanted to do the brand justice, and we were thinking of ways to do new things. I met with Celia, actually, just for a conversation. You never really know if someone’s going to be interested in working together. People are terrified by our timelines.

Textile designer Celia Birtwell with her partner and collaborator Ossie Clark in July 1971. Birtwell’s prints for Clark’s dresses are, in Daniel Lee’s words, “on every designer's moodboard.”

She came to the meeting saying, ‘You know, I’m really inspired by the check. I love the way Hockney paints ginghams on a tablecloth, the perspective that he gives to that.’ I said, ‘Well, would you be up for making some new work?’ And she did. She started with the checks, then the ginghams, and then the beautiful kind of English florals. Hockney gives me so much joy, emotion and warmth.

Birtwell’s new take on the brand’s check was inspired by the way David Hockney paints gingham on a tablecloth.

AW: Yeah, and he was so prolific, painting right up until the end, using an iPad, using different ways to make art. I’m sure you saw that last incredible show that was on at the Louis Vuitton Foundation in Paris. What a life. [Now] you’re meant to ask me…

DL: Congratulations on Vogue World: Milan. Would you like to talk about the robots?

AW: I’d love to. So the subject of Vogue World: Milan was our belief in the art of the human hand, the creativity of the hand, and the human mind in the age of technology. And we felt that to add something that represented technology, in a way that was — in my view — faintly ridiculous, reinforced the idea behind the theme of the exhibition. As is often in my case, not everyone agreed with me, but it certainly caused a lot of conversation.

Gigi Hadid at Vogue World: Milano. The show celebrated, in Anna Wintour’s words, “the art of the human hand” in the age of technology.

We’re moving on now to San Francisco in September, and we’re really going to be addressing the diversity and the incredible communities that live in San Francisco, and how it’s a city that has stood up for so much. The symphony and the museums there are extraordinary.

Talking about San Francisco, let’s talk about tech. Your last collection seemed to us that you were really advocating the celebration of imperfection and the romance of things made by hand. Is that true? And what do you feel about AI in terms of your creative work?

DL: As a child, I would spend my time making birthday cards, making cakes with my mom and making dance costumes for my sister. I’m a maker. Obviously I have a mobile phone, but tech is not a huge part of my life per se. I’m not a big computer gamer; I never even check email. I only really use WhatsApp.

DL: I think that’s what I love about luxury fashion. I really think luxury is about preservation of this savoir-faire, this craftsmanship. One of the main roles of the creative directors and companies today is to preserve that know-how and make it relevant, so that customers today can appreciate it.

OK, Anna, could you tell us more about next year’s Costume Institute show?

AW: Absolutely. It’s going to be extraordinary.

Daniel, I think it’s five years that you’ve been at Burberry?

AW: You went into a company that was in disarray, and looking at it from the outside, maybe not very well run. Two years ago, CEO Joshua Schulman came in. That must have been very welcome to have a good partner. He’s been integral — led by your creativity — to Burberry’s unbelievable turnaround. What is it like to work with Josh?

DL: Josh brought an incredible energy, passion, and belief in Burberry. He loves the brand, and his energy really reverberates in the company. I think that’s the role of a great leader. Josh brought a lot of discipline to the brand. He really grew up in American department stores; he intimately understands wholesalers and has very personal relationships with them.

Daniel Lee, Anna Wintour and Burberry CEO Joshua Schulman. Lee credits Schulman, who joined two years ago, with bringing “discipline” and a clear pricing strategy to the brand’s turnaround.

AW: I remember being in your store on a Saturday morning looking for something for a small child, and he was there, folding the scarves.

DL: We laugh, but Josh spends his vacations in malls. We had an executive dinner and were asked about our favorite places, and I’m sure he mentioned a mall in California. When he arrived, he brought a very clear idea around price architecture.

Anna, what do you think the British fashion industry needs at the moment?

AW: I think they need to really focus on who they are. We all look to London for creativity and individuality — and a degree of eccentricity. There’s a freedom to the way you see the kids dressed in the streets there that is the antithesis of American or cool Italian, more luxury dressing. It’s a little bit closer to what I was saying when I first was working in London, when you had to do everything.

I think that the British Fashion Council really needs to focus on that and make more noise about what you can see in London that you cannot see anywhere else. They have a great brand like Burberry, and it was so wonderful to see McQueen back in London and Christopher Kane at Mulberry.

They have so many creative kids, students, who can’t get jobs there, so they need to make sure that London becomes more of a global fashion mecca — that the retailers, the CEOs, and the journalists go. [Prime Minister] Andy Burnham seems like he’s going to be much more open to business in the UK, and they need to lean on what they own.

Burberry Spring/Summer 2027, a collection that celebrates handcraft and the brand’s 170th year.

So, the last shows were followed by quite a few creative director departures and appointments. How do you see this constant creative shuffle shaping the industry?

DL: My experience is that it takes time to understand and have a dialogue with the company that you work for, understand the archive, the culture, the people. It also takes time to build a team, and people need stability. I advocate for continuity. Also, when there are constant aesthetic shifts, it’s hard for the customer to understand that. I think there are moments where things do need to be revolutionized, and change is needed. Change is good. But too much change is discombobulating. It’s incredibly hard when you join a brand.

What do you think is the future of what we used to call magazines?

AW: I was doing an interview with Grace Coddington, who’s worked at Vogue for so many years, and we were reminiscing about when we were only working on print. She was able to go off to these extraordinary locations for what seems like an unthinkable amount of time — probably only with £20 in her pocket. She would go to Scotland for 10 days; she would go to China for two weeks. There was a great luxury in being able to have time to plan and think about what an issue of Vogue should look like. But it was a very narrow audience. When I first arrived at Vogue, people would disappear in the afternoons because they were going to Jones Beach — there just wasn’t that much to do.

Anna Wintour and Grace Coddington. Recalling their print days, Wintour remembers when Coddington could spend 10 days shooting in Scotland or two weeks in China. That was “a great luxury,” she says, but for a much narrower audience.

How lucky are we now to have all these amazing platforms to talk to our audiences? Our audiences have grown to unthinkable numbers. One of the great experiences and joys of what I do now is helping Adam [Baidawi, GQ’s global editorial director], Chloe [Malle, American Vogue’s head of editorial content], and Chioma [Nnadi, British Vogue’s head of editorial content], and all the editors that I work with over the world.

This afternoon, I’m leaving for Asia to work with our editors in Japan, China, Taiwan, and beyond. And I learn a lot from all of them. You have to be on the ground. I really feel that it’s so important to understand different cultures and how they think and work. I remember years and years ago, when I was first starting out, a great friend of mine said, ‘Anna, wherever you are, you have to walk in the street, climb a high point, visit a museum, and have a cup of coffee.’ I always remember that. I think sometimes when people get successful, they don’t walk in the street. When you walk in the street, that’s when you see the world.

What advice do you give those who want to become creative directors? Do you think social media has distorted the way young creatives see their trajectory by making them think they can be their own boss, or do you think it’s a good thing?

DL: I think social media makes things look very easy. People don’t always see the journey: the highs, the lows, the learnings. I don’t think you should set out to be an overnight success or to have instant gratification on social media. I’ve been every level, every part of a studio. I’ve been the intern, the pattern maker, the design director. I’ve lived all those jobs, and I’ve had those experiences, and that helps me do the job I do today.

AW: This is an audience of mostly executives. What’s one piece of advice you would give to them when it comes to working with creative teams?

DL: I think empathy is very important, respect is very important, understanding is important, and humility. No one’s right all the time. My favorite kind of working relationship is when it feels collaborative. I think as a creative leader, I try to create a space and framework to allow people to feel safe. I think this is something I once heard you say: ‘You hire great people, and you let them work.’ Trust is important.

#6669. The Gap Black Friday Sale Is a Holiday Miracle

The Gap Black Friday Sale kills two birds with one stone. The stone? Up to 60% off sitewide. The birds? Gifts for loved ones and gifts for you. Since its founding during the Summer of Love in the epicenter of the hippie revolution, the American fashion label has outfitted generations with stylish clothes both timely and timeless. And while it’s come a long way since its early days slinging Levi’s jeans and vinyl records, Gap’s designs are as relevant now as they were during Haight & Ashbury’s heyday. The prices, too, have remained accessible for the average American, even with inflation going insane.

Gap’s recent seasons have put itself back in the limelight, too, with the recent appointment of creative director Zac Posen as well as a string of killer collaborations and good ol’ fashioned Gap ads. Now that the best Black Friday clothing deals are here, you can score cartfuls of great menswear from hard-wearing denim to baby-soft cashmere sweaters—all for up to 60% off. But enough chatter. Here are just a handful of our favorites.

A lot of printed fleece can look a bit corny, IMO, but the fact that this one is a medium-pile with a very chill plaid in a good colorway makes me reconsider my stance.

Thermal tees are an easy hack for adding texture and warmth to your fit without getting too bulky. Extra points if it comes in a cool color, too.

Alright, alright, the Gap logo beanie is actually pretty cool.

This plus a beefy, broken-in hoodie, patched-up jeans, and heavy boots make for a 10/10 winter outfit.

Gap's main forte, in my opinion, is denim. Makes sense, since that's what the brand originally opened with. These heavyweight jeans are actually heavy and feel satisfyingly stiff, like a solid pair of Japanese denim for a fraction of the price.

If my math is correct, this is a great deal. And here's my work to prove it: $23 dupe > $5000 original.

Save for Supreme, few graphic hoodies have gone on to icon status like Gap's logo hoodie.

Perfect for layering over (or under!) everything this season.

Chunky-gauge rib knit, a proper tall zip-up neck, and a relaxed silhouette make this quarter-zip the stuff of '90s heartthrobs.

The polo cardigan is one of the great menswear hybrids that does everything well and this one in particular does it better than most.

The best things to buy at Gap? Start with the hits. The brand has been on a heater lately, mining its deep archive for all-star classics while dialing in modern silhouettes and workwear staples. Outerwear (especially the lighter layers), pants, shirts, sweaters, and sweats are all strong plays—especially if you haven’t checked in for a while.

This year in the US, Black Friday is on Friday, November 28, a day after Thanksgiving. While that’s the official date, many retailers roll out deals throughout November. You can expect the biggest discounts to happen between Thanksgiving and Cyber Monday, but be on the look out for retailers to launch sales early.

Cyber Monday lands on December 1 this year, the Monday after Thanksgiving. Most brands keep the deals rolling through the week—but don’t bank on it.

#6668. Alex Prager Has Hollywood Dreams

With a feature film and major solo shows, the artist is experiencing a moment like no other.

Alex Prager was in her cubicle at an internet startup, staring at the endless rows of other desks, when she realized that something was terribly wrong. “The rest of my life flashed in my mind,” she says. She began to cry. “It was like that Talking Heads song: And you may find yourself in a beautiful house / With a beautiful wife / And you may ask yourself, / ‘Well…how did I get here?’” she says. “This was not my life.” Soon after, she attended a show of William Eggleston’s work and left certain that her future was in photography. Within a week, she’d bought a used Nikon N90s camera and darkroom equipment. “I just knew, the way that you know you have a face and you know who you love. I knew from that moment forward what my path was,” she says.

It didn’t take long for Prager to start getting noticed in art circles. And this winter will be one of the most significant seasons of her career, with both a major solo museum show at the Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art in Bentonville, Arkansas, and an exhibition at the New York gallery Lehmann Maupin. DreamQuil, her first feature film, was released in theaters this fall and will be available to stream in December.

Prager’s color-saturated works capture cinematic scenes that bring to mind classic Hitchcock films. She creates full worlds for her photos, with sets, casts, and impeccable period costumes. Her pieces gained notice with her 2007 show “Polyester” at L.A.’s Robert Berman Gallery. The series showed women, perfectly attired in ’60s-era looks, posed in evocative ways. A heavily made-up girl clutches a Big Gulp, a flaxen braid thrown over one shoulder; four young women huddle together in swimsuits, a plane flying across the perfect blue sky above. An ominous feeling pervades.

Her work sparkles on the surface but explores something darker underneath. “The first color photograph I took was staged and a play on The Wizard of Oz and death, but it was very colorful and beautiful. I was interested in the way to explore something that felt layered. Underneath it, you find there are very uncomfortable things or darker stories and emotions,” Prager explains.

Prager steadily built up a following through a series of gallery shows, but things changed markedly in 2010 when her work was selected to be shown in the elite “New Photography” exhibit at MoMA. She had her first solo show at the Corcoran Gallery of Art in Washington, D.C., three years later. She’s also done work for magazines and brands like Cartier, Disney, and Apple.

“My work has always been about my personal challenges and things that I’m not really understanding in the world, but I think more and more it becomes less about me and my emotions. That’s probably also me becoming a mother and growing up, but the world has changed,” says Prager, whose son Francis is 9. The scale of her work has grown—bigger audiences, more ambitious concepts, a greater ability to stage elaborate photography—but the approach hasn’t. It’s still about the questions she needs answers to.

The idea for DreamQuil came to Prager during the pandemic (she was inspired by a meme that advertised YearQuil, a fictitious product that would allow people to sleep through the misery of 2020), and she wrote the script with her sister, Vanessa Prager. Elizabeth Banks stars as a woman who’s living in a depressing future world where people rarely leave their homes and finds herself dealing with her robot clone.

Opening two major shows within months of the release of her film wasn’t something Prager anticipated—each alone would have been a high point in her career—but she often does her best work amid a frenzy of activity. “I thrive in a bit of chaos,” she says. “I like to try to mold it and wrestle with it and attempt to control it and bend it to my will. It doesn’t always happen exactly the way I want, but it infuses me with inspiration and energy.”

#6666. 50 Percent of People In Relationships Would Take a Trip Together to Solve Their Problems

We may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love. Promise.

A “baecation” often entails a romantic getaway, passionate activities, and a lot of vacation sex. But what if traveling with your significant other meant a lot of difficult conversations, a heated back-and-forth, and working to fix your relationship. I know: this sounds nothing like the dreamy R&R you pictured—but for some couples, it’s exactly what they planned for.

According to Booking.com’s 2027 Travel Predictions, 58 percent of U.S. travelers said they would consider taking a trip to resolve conflicts or arguments.

Now, traveling itself already can cause real strain and arguments on relationships on its own. In the same data set, more than one-third of respondents said they found out they were incompatible with their companion after a trip. Nearly three in 10 people have considered ending a relationship or friendship over a trip, while more than one in five have actually cut a vacation short because of a bad travel companion.

But if you’re already having relationship issues with your partner, is a trip a good idea? People still seem to think so. About 81 percent said that taking part in at least one vacation activity with another person helps them have honest or difficult conversations.

So should you be planning a trip the next time you and your partner start arguing?

A change of scenery might be exactly what you and your partner need to see eye-to-eye again.

“Getting away from work, chores, kids, in-laws, or house and childcare stuff can lower defenses,” couples therapist Justena Kavanagh tells Cosmopolitan.

She explains that when you’re home, you’re essentially having every argument on the same “battleground.”

“Somewhere new often brings back the honeymoon period, when you could really see each other without life’s stresses in the way,” she says. And if both you and your partner have busy lives and packed schedules, a vacation may really be the only time you can focus on the issues in your relationship without distraction.

Plus, vacations encourage you to relax—which can go a long when in an argument. “When we’re rested, we’re more regulated, and when we’re regulated, we can listen instead of defending,” Kavanagh says.

She explains that it’s important to establish why exactly you’re going on the vacation in the first place. Are you getting away to talk about an issue? Or simple to get away from it and reconnect? Agreeing on the purpose for the trip before you start packing your bikini will help you and your partner get on the same page—so you don’t end up just arguing more later.

“Trips suit conversations about connection, like feeling distant, intimacy, or where the relationship is going,” she says. Other things like finances or in-law conflicts may need a follow-up at home.

If you decide that you’re going to talk your issues out, remember that you are still on vacation. That doesn’t mean everything has to be wonderful, of course. But Kavanagh encourages couples to treat the trip like a summit. This means talking early in the day (after a good night’s rest) and working on things while taking breaks.

The trip should essentially be your opportunity to discuss what’s currently happening in the relationship, where you want the relationship to go, and how to shift priorities to get there.

Sure, a beautiful view and hotel sex will definitely lighten the mood and probably even make you more agreeable—but it isn’t a magical bandaid for your relationship issues.

“If couples don’t have relational skills at home, they won’t miraculously have them on vacation,” Kavanagh warns.

So if you’re going to go on a vacation to work on things with your partner, you’re going to want to put a plan into place. The best method? Talking about the pattern behind the argument, rather than hyperfocusing on the latest incident.

And even if you do come to a resolution on vacation, make sure you’re setting a plan in place for the positive energy to flow into your everyday lives.

“Be realistic about home, where you’re more stressed and old patterns return fast,” Kavanagh says. “Plan follow-up support, a regular check-in, and what you’ll do when things go off track, because they will.”

Okay, so not all of us can afford to book a flight every time we get into an argument with our partner—but you don’t have to. Out of all the activities that people do on vacation, respondents said that it was mostly hikes or walking that was the most effective at getting them to open up and have the difficult conversations.

Lucky for you, taking a hike is totally free—and can do wonders for whatever issue you may be facing with your partner.

Kavanagh explains that walking and hiking take pressure off of an argument.

“Face to face can feel like a confrontation; side by side, you’re facing the same direction and don’t have to hold eye contact in the hardest moments,” she explains. This is something we see in psychotherapy: think about someone lying on a couch, looking at the ceiling. This helps physiologically and emotionally. Plus the actual physical activity helps, too.

“Walking also discharges stress and is a natural form of bilateral stimulation, the left-right rhythm used in therapies like EMDR,” she says.

When your partner is irritating you, it’s likely that the last thing you want to do is travel with them. But if you’re determined to move past whatever may be causing a rift, that might be exactly what you need.

Honeymoons and other happy occasions shouldn’t be the only time we travel with our partners with the purpose of growing closer, reconnecting, and strengthening the relationship. Sometimes, even in hardship, a little getaway could be the jumpstart your relationship needs to get back on track. Just remember that after the vacation ends, you do have to go back to reality.

“The good feelings are real, but the test is whether they last back home, where life is harder,” Kavanagh says.

#6662. 8 Reasons to Eat More Oatmeal

The humble oat is having something of a wellness renaissance. And while oatmeal may not be the most glamorous of breakfast foods, it’s definitely one of the healthiest. There’s a reason, after all, that oats have been eaten for thousands of years.

Dubbed “nature’s Ozempic” on social media right now, oats are enjoying a surge in popularity as interest in GLP-1 medications influences how we shop and eat. According to a new report from British supermarket Waitrose, as reported by The Guardian, sales of its Scottish oats have increased by 124% this year. There’s also the rise of so-called “fiber math”—the practice of incorporating more fiber into everyday meals through additions like chia seeds, nuts, and berries. And while no food can replicate the effects of prescription GLP-1 medications, oats are naturally rich in beta-glucan, a soluble fiber that supports gut health and helps us feel fuller for longer. Consider it a newfound appreciation for an age-old breakfast staple.

“I eat oatmeal every day,” says dermatologist and nutritionist Dr. Christian Merkel of the Skin and Laser Center in Munich, Germany. “For me, they are a real superfood—and totally underrated.” He notes that not only is oatmeal good for digestion—a key factor in overall health—but it also provides long-lasting feelings of satiety. Below, six reasons why oatmeal should be a regular star in your morning line-up.

“Oatmeal contains a large amount of fiber, which makes it very good for healthy digestion,” says Merkel. Oats contain both soluble and insoluble fiber: The former, most notably beta-glucan, absorbs water to form a gel-like substance in the digestive tract, while the latter helps add bulk to stools and promotes regular bowel movements. A half cup of dry rolled oats provides around four grams of fiber—a good head start on your recommended daily intake. To further boost the fiber content of your breakfast, try adding ground flaxseeds, chia seeds, raspberries, or chopped almonds. And remember to drink plenty of water throughout the day to help all that fiber do its job.

Oatmeal is a good source of vitamin K, which is essential for bone health and blood clotting. It also contains B vitamins—especially B1 (thiamine) and B5 (pantothenic acid)—which are essential for converting protein, carbohydrates, and fats into energy, supporting the digestive tract, making red blood cells, producing hormones, and for healthy skin and eyes.

“Studies have shown that oatmeal has been proven to lower cholesterol levels and can therefore also be beneficial against cardiovascular disease,” says Melker, noting that this is also thanks to beta-glucan, the soluble fiber in oats.

Oatmeal contains essential minerals such as copper, zinc, calcium, and potassium. It’s also rich in magnesium—important for energy, sleep, muscles, protein formation, the nervous system, genes, and more—and is especially high in the inflammation-reducing trace mineral manganese.

Oats are a great plant-based source of protein. “If you compare the nutritional values of different types of grains, you will find that the values of oatmeal are excellent,” says Merkel, noting that this helps balance out the carbohydrates. “The protein content is very good at 5.3 grams per half cup.”

Though some glucose-experts disagree, Merkel says oatmeal is a safe option for those wishing to keep their blood sugar in check. “There is virtually no sugar in oatmeal which means that your insulin level will not rise quickly when you eat oatmeal,” he says. “Instead, there is a very slight, healthy rise in blood sugar and therefore long-lasting satiety.” Additionally, oats have been shown to lower blood sugar levels—especially in people with obesity or who have type 2 diabetes—thanks to good ol’ beta-glucan’s ability to slow the emptying of the stomach.

Oats have something of an edge over other grains when it comes to antioxidants. They contain a distinctive group of naturally occurring plant compounds called avenanthramides, which researchers have identified as having antioxidant and potential anti-inflammatory properties. While more research is needed to understand their effects on human health, they offer another reason to appreciate the nutritional complexity of the humble oat. For an extra hit of antioxidants at breakfast, top your oatmeal with blueberries, raspberries, or a sprinkling of cinnamon.

Your morning bowl of oatmeal is also breakfast for the beneficial bacteria in your gut. The fiber in oats acts as a prebiotic, feeding gut bacteria that, in turn, produce compounds called short-chain fatty acids. These play an important role in maintaining the intestinal barrier and supporting immune function. A study published in 2026 in Nature Communications also explored how interactions between oats and the gut microbiome may contribute to their cholesterol-lowering effects. To make your morning oatmeal even more gut-friendly, try adding a spoonful of live-culture yogurt or kefir for a combination of prebiotics and probiotics.

Be sure to choose steel-cut whole oats instead of instant oats, which have less fiber and nutrients. Choose organic if possible. And, “bear in mind that a large proportion of the vitamins and trace elements are broken down during the cooking process,” says Merkel, who adds that the healthiest way to eat oats is actually “uncooked.” If that sounds a little too rustic for you, he recommends the two alternatives below:

To make the overnight oats, place oats in a small bowl and pour in a plant-based drink of your choice until the oats are completely covered. “Personally, I’m a big fan of unsweetened almond milk because it has the best nutritional value of all plant-based drinks and the taste also appeals to most people,” says Merkel, who recommends enhancing the oats with nutritionally-rich spices such as cinnamon and turmeric. “Turmeric is rich in antioxidants and just a teaspoon is enough to make breakfast even healthier,” he says. Cover the oats and leave them to soak in the refrigerator for eight to twelve hours. “In the morning, you can add another superfood in the form of blueberries. Dark berries are also rich in antioxidants,” suggests Merkel. “If you prepare your oatmeal in this way, you have a super healthy breakfast that is rich in fiber and antioxidants and, unlike packaged muesli, only gently raises your insulin levels and keeps you full for a long time.”

Merkel says oats can be easily added to your usual protein shake or smoothie for a boost of extra protein, nutrients, and fiber. “Add one to two tablespoons of uncooked rolled oats and some fresh fruit into the blender. The oats give the shake a pleasantly nutty taste and the vitamins are retained during the blending process,” he says.

#6657. 16 Festive Holiday Date Ideas for the Most Wonderful Time of Year

Iam here to debunk a common dating myth: Despite what all the relationship gurus might suggest, dating doesn’t have to be confined to the summer. In fact, some of the best, most romantic dates can happen during the late fall and dead of winter. After all, every street and tree is covered in twinkling lights and the cold weather gives you an excuse (not that you need one) to cozy up next to your crush. Add the festivities of the holiday season on top of all of that and you literally have the makings of a dream date.

Sure, the urge to snuggle up with your coziest blanket and binge your favorite rom-coms is nagging you and your person—I get it. But this holiday season is the time to make your Hallmark movie dreams a reality! Whether you’re looking for an option for a third date with someone you just started seeing or trying to keep things fresh and fun in your long-term relationship, there’s something on this list for you.

Volunteering as a date night is a great way to see someone’s generous side. Find a local donation center, soup kitchen, or a cause that means a lot to you. You’ll be able to tell a lot about your date by their reaction to this idea and how they carry themselves throughout the volunteering.

This one will really test your teamwork. You can either grab a premade kit or go old-school and use a pint-sized milk carton and graham crackers as your base. Some of the premade are pretty simple, while others can be a bit more intricate. Either way, both will force you and your date to work together and problem solve. This will be a good way for those red flags or green flags to show themselves.

Because it’s time you get in on the whole matching pajamas and Santa hats. If you don’t want to put out money for a photographer, set up your phone’s camera with a timer and tripod—the photos can look just as amazing!

Elevate your hot chocolate game with fun flavors, like salted caramel, dark chocolate, or peppermint. You can buy premade variety packs or really chef it up with making your own. Whatever you choose, just be sure not to skim on the toppings. Grab marshmallows of all sizes, candy canes, whipped cream (I personally love the boozy vodka-infused peppermint one from Whipshots), and whatever else sounds enticing. You will be chocolate wasted and it will be fantastic.

Karaoke isn’t about who sounds the best but who has the best energy. Belt out your favorite holiday jams, from the classics to new renditions of the season’s most popular songs. It’s truly a perfect way to bond and see if your date can match your vibe.

This option is such a fun way to spend time together. Whether this is an early date with someone you recently started seeing or an activity you and your longtime love do, it’s great for talking, asking questions, and having fun. If you’re a part of the first group, this can be an opportunity to make a candle for each other—then you could exchange them as a low-stakes holiday gift (because getting a present for your situationship is always tricky).

If you or your date are people who appreciate a good aesthetic, finding a local light show could be the perfect night out. The low lighting and colorful moments can help you draw closer to your person, whether it’s in the car riding through or walking. Light shows leave room for more intimate conversations to take place, too, if you want that.

The best way to spread holiday cheer is by supporting local businesses. From small batch food to unique clothes and accessories, it’s where you and your partner can shop for each other or grab gifts for loved ones. Oftentimes, these events also have other activities available nearby, like ice skating or photo moments, making for the perfect two-in-one date.

Bring out the creative energy with a cutesy arts and crafts moment. Grab a few blank ornaments, brushes and bottles of paint, stickers, fabric, and whatever else strikes your fancy. Set it all up on a flat surface (like a dining table or floor), throw in a few Christmas songs and snacks, and you’ve got the makings of a simple and fun at-home holiday date night.

Speaking of not making date night complicated, a simple stroll through your neighborhood (or perhaps one that’s more festive than yours) can still be made special. Make some boozy hot chocolates or hotty toddies, strap in to all your cold-weather gear, and sidewalk hike through your community. Bonus points for lots of hand holding, hugging, kissing and gossiping about the neighbors inflatable holiday characters in their front yard.

“Do you want to build a snowman?” Anna from Frozen isn’t the only one who can enjoy the feeling of holiday magic. Similar to ornament decorating and gingerbread house making, building a snowman is the ultimate nostalgia cheat code. While he might not come to life like Olaf, dressing him up with the cutest scarf and hat will still be just as worthwhile.

The intentionality behind handwritten notes will forever show true thoughtfulness. This idea allows the two of you to really get creative with one another and reflect on who in your lives you want to wish a happy holiday season. Whether you’re sending our joint cards or individual ones, let your heartfelt emotions shine through.

Can you technically do this any time of the year? Yes. But walk with me: What makes sporting events special for the holiday season is the amount of on-the-ground activations and curated experiences that teams provide fans. I’m talking seasonal menus galore, holiday-themed lounges, and activations where you can put your partner’s competitive skills to the test. It’s almost like a bunch of dates in one!

Warm up from the brisk cool air outside by attending a wine tasting at your local winery or private holiday-themed events. Wines with notes of cocoa, hints of spice, and earthiness are especially great to lean into for rich flavor. They also pair well with heavier meals that people typically enjoy during the winter months.

Love the snow but hate the cold? Search for the nearest igloo dining restaurant near you for a winter lunch or dinner. Usually, the igloos are kind of snug (but not in an uncomfortable way), giving you at-home levels of cozy with a space heater or bonfire. They’re also super festive with the decor, so you and your date will feel all the holiday cheer.

#6654. How to Read ‘The Hunger Games’ Books in Order of Release

We may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love. Promise.

In the mood to read some Hunger Games books after seeing Sunrise on the Reaping in theaters? Maybe you never visited Panem on the page in the first place. Here’s your guide to how to read Suzanne Collins’s dystopian young adult book series in order. (Remember, even though there are six movies, there are only five books.)

Collins’s trilogy was published in a timely succession back in the day. Then a decade passed, and all of a sudden the author surprised us with a new installment. Are there more Hunger Games books on the horizon? We certainly hope so. But for now, let’s be grateful for what we have.

In the world of young adult fiction, “what if you had to fight to the death with the boy in your class who has a crush on you” is about as perfect as premises get. The emotional stakes are as high as the external stakes. Katniss Everdeen was a survivalist before she volunteered to replace her younger sister in her dystopian society’s televised child slaughter. She could hunt and forage better than most of the people in her Appalachian hometown. What she didn’t know how to do was smile for the cameras and perform for the crowd if that’s what it takes to survive.

Katniss returns to District 12 in a PR relationship with her fellow tribute, victor, and ally Peeta Mellark. They’re miserable on the victory tour, unable to process their feelings and seeing the consequences of their actions everywhere. Then, a year later, President Snow announces that the third Quarter Quell will be Hunger Games: All Stars. The tributes are all former winners and adults. Are Katniss and Peeta simply back where they started? Not really. This time they have allies, and plans to finally move against the Capitol.

In the final book of the original trilogy, Katniss is being dressed up and manipulated for the cameras yet again. But it’s not the Capitol doing it this time. It’s the rebellion, led by the secret District 13. It’s scary to think about how even if you believe in the cause, you may find yourself using the same methods as your enemy. War has broken out in Panem, and Katniss and Peeta are separated. So much happens in this book that they had to split it into two movies.

Ten years later, Collins returned with a fascinating subject for a new prequel: the 10th Hunger Games, during which a teenaged Coriolanus Snow mentored District 12’s lost victor, Lucy Gray Baird, and fell in love with her while brainstorming how to get the murder reality show better ratings with his classmates. Their romance is not really one that you can root for, because we know we can’t fix him. He had bad vibes all along. But it’s a fascinating, twisted tale of how the Hunger Games as we know it came to be.

Next, of course, Collins answered fandom prayers by writing a Haymitch Abernathy prequel. We now know the story of every single District 12 victor’s games. Background details link District 12 women like Lucy Gray and Maysilee Donner to Katniss Everdeen in fun ways. It also serves as a nice companion to Catching Fire, with many appearances from the victors Katniss and Peeta meet during their own Quarter Quell. But be careful what you wish for, because this is a brutal and bloody book about the many ways the Capitol can edit and control your story using propaganda.

The party line is that Suzanne Collins writes when she is inspired to write, and not a second before. As of the release of the film adaptation of Sunrise on the Reaping, there has not been a new book announcement. But that hasn’t stopped the theories.

In the fandom, the character who probably has the most support in this realm is Finnick Odair. He’s sexy, confident, and has a tragically beautiful love story with Annie Cresta, a fellow victor from his district. They were also Career tributes. The districts that chose to buy into the Hunger Games by training children to kill haven’t been explored in depth in the books. There’s definitely potential there for a socially relevant story. What is that process like from the inside? Do they have stage moms? I am all for this, but just have one note: let’s tell it from Annie’s POV.

But there are so many other avenues that a future Hunger Games book could take. Collins could write about Cinna and the world of the stylists. That could include an update on President Snow’s cousin Tigris. She could leave the games behind and write a book about District 13. (Alma Coin origin story, divas?) What about the unknown, presumably dead victor of the first Quarter Quell? There’s also the Dark Days and the first rebel uprising in Panem. I wouldn’t mind a Plutarch story, as well...but I really think we need to hear from a female character this time.

Cyber Monday lands on November 30 this year, the Monday after Thanksgiving. Most brands keep the deals rolling through the week—but that doesn't mean a deal will last all day, so act fast.

Are deals better on Black Friday or Cyber Monday?

Black Friday and Cyber Monday offer equally good clothing deals. Plan for large retailers and more-established brands to offer deals on Black Friday, and smaller menswear boutiques to hold out for Cyber Monday. As a baseline, expect the better Black Friday sales to start at 20% off and go upwards from there. In the lead up to Black Friday, also be on the lookout for the coveted sale on sale, which has become the norm in recent years.

#6651. The Opera Coat Is Everywhere—Here’s the Chinese Influence Behind the Trend

A moment to appreciate the history of the trending piece.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

It’s been living rent-free in my mind for the better part of this year: Conner Ives’s silk brocade opera coat, which captured nearly every fashion lover’s heart when it debuted on the fall/winter 2026 runway at London Fashion Week. Reminiscent of Mary-Kate Olsen’s fur-trimmed Balmain coat from the 2013 Met Gala, this particular stunner, along with the designer’s other iterations, seems to be what every It girl is wearing.

The coat—crafted with silk tapestries dating back to the Qing dynasty and with hand-embroidered depictions of red-crowned cranes, bamboo leaves, and flowers—was undoubtedly the first wave in what would become a tsunami of a trend: opera coats. And while plenty of faux fur-trimmed coats have made their way onto the market, those featuring Chinese imagery like that on Ives’s iterations have taken center stage.

“There’s been a real change in how people perceive Chinese design,” Cheryl Leung, founder and creative director of Sau Lee, tells ELLE. Leung attributes the opera coat’s rise in popularity to fashion’s shift away from minimalism and consumers’ growing appetite for expressive pieces, richer fabrics, and textures. “Brocade is a great example because it has so much character,” she says. “The fabrics can be quite ornate, but when you put them into a modern silhouette or style them with something very simple, they feel completely different.”

Chinese design has often been presented through a Western lens, but designers like Leung and Kim Shui are creating work rooted in their own cultural perspectives. Shui, the Chinese-American, New York-based creative director behind her eponymous label, has long been drawn to Chinese garments and the ways they communicate identity. “I’m particularly interested in the visual language and craftsmanship of traditional Chinese garments, whether it’s the silhouette of the qipao (a traditional Chinese dress dating back to the Qing dynasty), the richness of brocade, or traditional techniques like embroidery and intricate knot closures,” Shui tells ELLE. “I look at these elements not as things to reproduce literally, but as a vocabulary that I can reinterpret.”

While the trend has gained widespread popularity, the Chinese design details behind it can sometimes be overlooked. “I’ve seen so many ‘trending winter coat’ videos featuring Chinese brocade coats with fur trim and traditional Chinese embroidered silk coats, but they don’t make any reference to their Chinese origins,” Shui says. “Instead of using terms like ‘qipao’ or ‘mandarin collar,’ creators will often describe these details generically as a ‘stand collar’ or ‘high neckline.’ It’s important to acknowledge where these design elements come from and the history behind them—why erase the cultural context?”

Leung sees the coat’s popularity as an opportunity to bring attention to its history and the designers reinterpreting it. Shui and her team have also been creating content about the histories of brocade, embroidery, and the qipao, as well as the cultural references behind her collections to bring more awareness of the craft to her audience.

“I do think there’s a difference between appreciating a design tradition and overlooking where it came from,” Leung says. “If a designer has been inspired by Chinese textiles, craftsmanship, or traditional clothing, acknowledging that doesn’t take anything away from their creativity. If anything, it gives the work more depth and helps people appreciate the original references.” Shui adds that brands outside the culture have a “responsibility to acknowledge their origins rather than presenting them as an entirely new aesthetic.”

Fashion has been both a vehicle for cultural exchange and a product of it—and trends will undoubtedly come and go. Not everyone will be interested in the cultural history of the piece they buy—and Leung doesn’t necessarily think they need to be. Shui is happy to see people from all backgrounds embrace garments from outside of their own cultures. “I hope this renewed interest encourages people to look beyond the garment itself and discover the rich traditions and craftsmanship behind it,” she says.

#6646. I Tested Peloton's New, More Affordable Folding Treadmill

In my mind and, I think the minds of many others, Peloton has always been a stationary bike brand. The Bike, after all, was its first product, turning the Peloton name into a catch-all term for at-home cycling that we now hear everywhere, from broadcasts of the Tour de France and Giro d'Italia to television sitcoms. (A running gag online is that Peloton's upscale, soothing video workout content is worlds away from The Office's Dwight Schrute leading a group of stationary riders off an imaginary cliff.)

Nevertheless, Peloton actually has been making treadmills since 2018. The first Tread delivered the same proposition as the Bike: premium hardware that looks good enough to bring out of the basement, as well as access to interactive, instructor-led runs and HIIT classes on a big, immersive screen. Over the years, Peloton has brought improvements to that first Tread: larger screens, voice controls, AI-informed movement tracking for form analysis and coaching.

The new Tread Flex, however, heads in a slightly different direction. It has a simpler belt, simpler speakers, a smaller screen. It's $1,300 cheaper than the next step up, and $4,500 cheaper (!) than Peloton's slat belt-equipped Tread+ Vision. Its affordability isn't even its main selling point, however, because the Tread Flex has a nifty final trick: it folds up to save space.

Could these space and money-saving tactics make the Tread as popular as the Bike? Well, I run nearly every day, and ever since a tester Tread Flex showed up at my door, I've been doing it indoors much more frequently. In my experience, here's what makes Peloton's latest worth considering.

Treadmills tend to have a problem that stationary bikes don't: the nicer they get, the bigger they get. Premium models have larger motors and roomier running platforms. In short, they're heavy. (The Tread+ Vision is a hefty 460 pounds.) The Tread Flex is 170 pounds less, and that's crucial to its ability to fold up, because that feature wouldn't be much of a selling point if it felt like adding a power clean to the end of every run.

In reality, stowing the Tread Flex is quite easy. You just lift up the running deck from the end and push it forward until a hydraulic cylinder locks into place. There's a pin clip to lock it. To drop it down, you push forward on the deck and then on the hydraulic support, then walk it back. At about 45 degrees, the hydraulics take over completely; you can go put on your running shoes while a gentle thump lets you know the deck is back on the ground.

Folding up the Tread Flex drops its area from about 16.5 square feet to half that. (The Tread+ Vision is around 19.25.) Just as importantly, I've discovered, is that lifting the deck brings the machine up onto a set of locking wheels. I've kept mine in a designated corner, but it's so easy to move that it wouldn't be much hassle to wheel it out and lower it for every workout, if your space required it. Get your cardio out of the way, then get your cardio out of the way.

Okay, so folding and moving a treadmill might be a pain if you're using it every day. But I suspect if you're running that often, you're doing some of it outside. I live less than an hour away from the Canadian border, and run on roads and trails five or six times a week all year round. Good layers get you pretty far, and there's a reason why run clubs continue to boom while SoulCycle-adjacent Mile High Run Club closed all its studios this year.

Treadmills are for something else. They're for a warm-up prior to lifting, or for bootcamp-style HIIT workouts that combine sprinting intervals with weight intervals. The prioritization value of time spent doing these doesn't seem to align with the space investment a treadmill requires if you don't have a pool house or big garage. (I have a sun porch-slash-mudroom where I keep firewood and ski boots in the winter and a napping couch in the summer.)

This is how, I think, the Tread Flex makes the ultimate proposition as the ideal home treadmill. A treadmill doesn't replace a usual running routine; it adds to it. On Monday I do my usual seven miles down the road and back on the river trails; on Tuesday I let Andy Speer kick my ass with sprints and kickstand deadlifts. (And, sure, when it's -10° and blowing in late January, I might run inside, now that I have the option.)

None of the above would matter as much if it came at the cost of quality. I've run on hotel treadmills that sound like your grandma's washing machine and feel similar to how they look, i.e., stomping around on hollow plastic. The Tread Flex may not have the cushioned slat belt the Tread+ Vision has, but it's definitely not that.

What it does have is a spec that's right in line with top-notch treadmills. Its max speed is 12.5 miles per hour (a 4:48 mile, in runner's units), a 12.5% max incline grade (but no decline), and a 20-inch by 59-inch running surface that, though not cushioned, feels good to run on. The swiveling screen is nice and big at 21.5 inches, with HD resolution and a touchscreen interface. I particularly like how adjusting speed and incline is done with rolling knobs, which feel much better—and more natural—to engage with than buttons when you're gasping at threshold pace.

On top of that is Peloton's interactive experience: You can take live classes where you can pit yourself against others and get kudos from the instructor. The pre-recorded catalogue includes thousands of classes for yoga, Pilates, and meditation, in addition to strength and the running, cycling, and rowing the company makes machines for.

The Tread Flex also provides personalized training plans, smart pacing guidance based on where you're at, automatically adjusting incline for classes, and of course leaderboards and an entire ecosystem of badges and achievements to earn, if you're into all that. For $50 per year, that is.

Oh, and did I mention it's a good-looking machine? It's sleek; an attractive, soft-edged Z with a minimal screen instead of a board of colorful buttons. Nobody's throwing around the word "console" to describe this thing. That's good; home gym setups deserve different consideration than gym rigs. If images of Crunch Fitness flash through your head every time you glance into the corner, something has missed the mark.

Where Peloton's Tread Vision treadmills are clearly high-end, the Tread Flex toes the line against mainstream consumer models. Its features match up with some of the most popular machines, and its price, while at the higher end of the spectrum, does too. But the Tread Flex gets there with more style, and with Peloton's huge ecosystem of live and archived class content.

So, if we're looking at other treadmills out there, my quick answer is yes. The Tread Flex is the utilitarian Peloton Treadmill, but it's still a Peloton treadmill.

How you answer this question really requires asking yourself a series of other questions first. What do you want a treadmill for? How much do you want to invest? Do you want access to fitness classes—especially ones other than running—and are you okay with the $50/month subscription fee?

Form factor and access to classes and content are non-negotiables. The Tread Flex might be Peloton's new entry-level treadmill, but it's far from a simple running machine. Flex refers to that nifty fold-up feature, but also to this treadmill's ability to integrate into an exercise program that also includes strength training, HIIT workouts, yoga, and on and on.

As a runner who prefers to log miles outside whenever possible, I was encouraged by how much I enjoyed running on the Tread Flex. The classes are fun, and Peloton's instructors are real pros, but even in Just Run mode, the Tread Flex proved responsive and comfy. It's getting dark around 4:30 PM these days, and my daylight windows for running on the well-used roads around me have narrowed like a Death Star trash compactor. It's nice to know I can snag seven miles after sundown if need be.

Well, if you aren't limited by space or cash, the Tread Vision and Tread+ Vision get you bigger screens, AI-enabled running form feedback and coaching, and a more cushioned, broader running area. If you just prefer running or walking on a treadmill to doing it outside, investing more heavily in a treadmill is worth considering (though the Tread Flex will still be great).

The Tread Flex's real competition is the NordicTrack Commercial 1750, which you'll find recommended on just about every treadmill buying guide on the internet. The machines are similar in function and specs, but there are some differences. The NordicTrack's running surface is two inches wider and one inch longer; it has a slightly more powerful motor; it can decline to -3% grade; its belt is slightly cushioned; it has a built-in fan; and NordicTrack's class and entertainment platform, iFit, is cheaper at $39 a month.

In comparison, the Tread Flex takes up slightly less space, has a higher max speed (12.5 mph over 12 mph), a steeper incline (12.5% over 12%), and a larger screen (21.5 inches over 16 inches). The rolling knobs to adjust speed and incline are nicer to use. My partner, who designs commercial and residential interior spaces, agrees with me that the Tread Flex is a better-looking machine.

List price for the Tread Flex is $300 cheaper, but the NordicTrack seems to be perpetually on sale. So it might come down to looks, that 3% decline, or what class platform you'd like to buy into.
