#6626. An All-Time Great Air Jordan Is Returning on Black Friday

Sit still for a second. The birds are singing. The sun is shining. The Air Jordan 4 ‘Bred’ is returning. Nature is healing. Everything, for once, is exactly where it should be.

The ‘Bred’ (short for “black and red”) is one of the original Air Jordan 4 colorways from 1989. Created by legendary Nike designer Tinker Hatfield, it came in slick black nubuck with hits of gray and red throughout. Michael Jordan famously wore a pair when he hit The Shot over Craig Ehlo to knock the Cleveland Cavaliers out of the 1989 NBA Playoffs—so, yeah, there’s a bit of lore there too.

Unsurprisingly, Jordan Brand has brought it back a few times over the past few years. There was a retro in 1999, followed by versions in 2008 and 2012, and then another in 2019, which finally brought the OG “Nike Air” branding back to the heel. Then, in 2024, we got the ‘Bred Reimagined,’ which swapped the classic nubuck for leather. The less said about that one, the better.

Because two years later, Jordan Brand is going back to the good stuff. The ‘Bred’ is decked out in black nubuck again, with gray eyelets, red accents around the sole, and the all-important “Nike Air” stamped across the back. Even the Nike branding on the outsole is returning. Basically, if you looked at the ‘Bred Reimagined’ and thought, “Look how they massacred my boy,” congrats: this one's for you.

And there’s something quite nice about that. The AJ4 has been messed with, remixed, collabed on, and reworked in just about every way possible over the last few years. Some of those experiments have been great! Some… not so much. The ‘Bred’ doesn’t really need any of that. It’s been one of the best Air Jordans on the planet for 37 years. If it ain’t broke, don’t fix it.

The Air Jordan 4 ‘Bred’ is set to drop on November 27 via Nike, the SNKRS app, and select stockists globally.

#6625. Steak Bites With Spinach Couscous

A traditional steak dinner can feel like too much for a weeknight: too expensive, too likely to trip the smoke alarm, too fussy to cook to a perfect medium-rare. But cut a steak into bite-size pieces and suddenly it transforms into a quick-cooking protein that’s no more demanding than chicken breast or tofu. Rub the steak with the spices and make the quick no-recipe yogurt sauce a few hours ahead if it’s helpful with time management. To account for the extra liquid thrown off by the spinach as it cooks, the water-to-couscous ratio in this recipe differs from that often found on the back of the bag (or box) so measure accordingly.

More quick dinners this way: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps; Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry; and Easy Fish Tacos With Spicy Sauce.

Place 1–1¼ lb. boneless New York strip steak (1–1½" thick), cut into 1" pieces, 1 Tbsp. dried oregano, 2 tsp. onion powder, 2 tsp. sugar, and 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl; season generously with freshly ground pepper and toss to coat. Let sit at least 10 minutes or cover and chill up to 8 hours (no need to bring to room temperature before cooking if chilling).

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven with a tight-fitting lid over medium. Add 1 bunch scallions, thinly sliced, ½ cup finely chopped dill, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; cook, stirring occasionally, until scallions are softened, about 5 minutes. Add 10 oz. baby spinach in 2–3 handfuls, stirring and letting wilt slightly after each addition before adding more, 5–7 minutes total. Pour in 1 cup water and bring to a boil; season with more salt if needed. Add 1 cup Moroccan couscous and stir to break up any lumps. Remove from heat; quickly cover with lid and let sit 10 minutes.

Meanwhile, heat 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet, preferably cast iron, over high. Arrange steak in a single layer; cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 6–8 minutes. Reduce heat to medium; continue to cook, stirring often, until meat is just cooked through, about 1 minute more. Remove from heat. Add remaining 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; toss to combine. (Residual heat from pan will cook out any raw garlic flavor.)

Uncover couscous and fluff with a fork to separate grains. Spoon into a large shallow bowl or onto a platter. Top with steak. Cut 1 lemon into quarters and squeeze juice from 1 quarter over steak. Scatter thinly sliced cucumber and some dill sprigs on top; drizzle with oil.

Combine 1 cup plain whole-milk yogurt and a generous pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl; squeeze juice from 2 lemon quarters into yogurt. Stir to combine. If sauce is thick, stir in water, a spoonful at a time, to loosen.

Serve steak and couscous with yogurt sauce and remaining lemon quarter and more lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6624. BA's Best Lasagna

This lasagna recipe has “rainy Sunday cooking project” written all over it. Layers of slow-cooked pork-and-beef ragù, silky Parmesan béchamel, and pasta bake into a rich, creamy lasagna Bolognese with a browned top and crisp edges. Make the sauces ahead to break up the work, or settle in for a day of very good kitchen smells.

The secret weapon is the meat sauce. Why make meatballs only to break them apart? Searing the meat in large balls leaves room for moisture to escape, so you get deep browning instead of a potful of steam. After a long, gentle braise, a potato masher turns them into ragù. Whole canned tomatoes, crushed by hand, give you control over the sauce’s chunky texture.

One step you can skip: boiling the noodles. In side-by-side retests, regular dried lasagna noodles (not no-boil!) produced similar results whether parboiled or layered straight from the box. The ragù and béchamel provide enough moisture to cook the pasta in the oven—as long as every noodle is covered. Spread the sauces to the edges, leaving no dry patches, and making sure the sauce totally covers the top layer of noodles before baking. Round it out with homemade garlic bread and a Caesar salad.

Do I need to buy no-boil lasagna noodles?

No—use regular dried lasagna noodles, preferably De Cecco. Skipping the boiling step isn’t the same as using noodles labeled “no-boil.” In our original tests, those absorbed too much sauce, leaving the finished lasagna drier than we wanted.

Why doesn’t this lasagna have ricotta or mozzarella?

This is a lasagna Bolognese, built around meat ragù and Parmesan-enriched béchamel rather than a separate cheese filling. The béchamel supplies the creaminess, while Parmesan brings salty, nutty flavor. For a less involved version with a cheese filling, try our Cottage Cheese Lasagna.

What’s the best way to split up the work?

Make the ragù one day, then tackle the béchamel, assembly, and baking the next. For an even lighter second day, make both sauces ahead and refrigerate them separately; rewarm the béchamel just enough to loosen it before layering. The ragù can be refrigerated for up to 4 days or frozen for up to 3 months, while the béchamel can be refrigerated for 1 day.

Save recipes and plan every week with confidence. Download the app

Saving this cooking project for another day? We tasted nine brands to find the best frozen lasagna.

Preheat oven to 225°. Mix 2 lb. ground pork and 1 lb. ground beef chuck (20% fat) with your hands in a large bowl; season generously with kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper, then mix again. Form into about 18 large meatballs (they don’t need to be perfect—you’ll be mashing them later).

Warm 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium-high heat. Working in 2 batches, cook meatballs, turning occasionally and reducing heat if bottom of pot looks in danger of scorching, until browned all over, about 6 minutes per batch. Transfer to a rimmed baking sheet as they’re done.

Reduce heat to medium. Add 2 oz. pancetta (Italian bacon) or slab bacon, chopped, to pot and cook, stirring often, until lightly browned and beginning to crisp, about 5 minutes. Add 1 medium onion, finely chopped, 1 celery stalk, finely chopped, 1 medium carrot, peeled, finely chopped, and 6 garlic cloves, sliced, and cook, stirring occasionally, until vegetables are softened, 6–8 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. tomato paste and cook, stirring constantly, until paste is darkened in color, about 2 minutes.

Add ¾ cup dry white wine and cook, stirring occasionally, until almost completely evaporated, about 5 minutes. Add one 28-oz. can whole peeled tomatoes, crushing with your hands, and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, stirring occasionally, until liquid is jammy and reduced by about half, 8–10 minutes. Add 1 cup low-sodium chicken broth and 1 cup whole milk, then return meatballs to pot. Bring to a simmer. Cover pot partially with a lid, transfer to oven, and cook, checking every hour or so to ensure liquid is at a low simmer and adjusting oven temperature as needed, until meatballs are falling-apart tender, 3–4 hours.

Using a potato masher, break meatballs apart and incorporate into liquid (you should have about 8 cups ragù; transfer pot to stovetop and simmer gently to reduce if needed). Taste and season with more salt and black pepper if needed.

Do ahead: Ragù can be made 4 days ahead. Let cool; cover and chill, or freeze up to 3 months.

Melt 7 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large saucepan over medium heat. Whisk in ¼ cup plus 3 Tbsp. all-purpose flour and cook, whisking occasionally, until mixture smells slightly nutty, about 4 minutes. Whisking constantly, add 6 cups whole milk. Increase heat to medium-high and continue whisking until mixture comes to a simmer. Reduce heat to maintain a simmer and cook, whisking occasionally, until béchamel thickens, about 4 minutes. Continue cooking, whisking occasionally and adjusting heat as needed to maintain a gentle simmer, until béchamel is smooth and velvety, 8–10 minutes more. Remove from heat and whisk in 4 oz. Parmesan cheese, coarsely grated (about 1 cup), a pinch of cayenne pepper, and a pinch of ground nutmeg. (You should have about 6 cups béchamel.) Season with kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper. Transfer to a large bowl and press plastic wrap directly onto surface; let cool slightly.

Note: You can skip the following boiling step (and save yourself a pot to wash!). In side-by-side retests, the BA Test Kitchen found that regular dried lasagna noodles (not no-boil) produced similar results whether parboiled or layered straight from the box. To use them uncooked, spread the ragù and béchamel all the way to the edges, covering every noodle completely, and make sure the sauce blankets the top layer of noodles before baking.

If parboiling: Cook 1¼ lb. dried lasagna noodles in a large pot of boiling salted water, stirring occasionally and separating them so they don’t stick together, until just starting to soften but still snap in half rather than bend when folded; 3 minutes is the magic number. The noodles will be so firm it will just seem all wrong. Using tongs, transfer noodles to a large bowl of cold water to cool. Drain and lay flat in a single layer on a rimmed baking sheet, separated by parchment or wax paper.

Lightly coat a 13x9", 4–6-qt. glass or ceramic baking dish with extra-virgin olive oil. Spread 1½ cups ragù in dish. Lay a single layer of noodles over ragù (cut or break noodles as needed to fill any gaps). Spoon 1¼ cups béchamel over noodles, spreading in an even layer with a small offset spatula. Top béchamel with 1½ cups of meat sauce. Repeat layering noodles, béchamel, and ragù 3 more times. Top with a fifth layer of noodles and the remaining 1 cup béchamel.

Note: For more pasta in every bite, build six layers instead of five. Start with the same 1½ cups ragù on the bottom of the dish, but use 1 cup béchamel and 1¼ cups ragù between the pasta layers. Finish with a sixth layer of pasta and the remaining 1 cup béchamel.

Cover with a lightly oiled piece of aluminum foil and set lasagna pan on a rimmed baking sheet (just to catch drips). Bake lasagna until bubbling gently around the edges, about 1 hour. Remove from oven. Increase oven temperature to 425° and carefully place rack in top of oven. Remove foil from lasagna and continue to bake until top is browned and crisp around the edges, 10–15 minutes longer. Let sit 10 minutes before serving.

Do ahead: Béchamel can be made 1 day ahead; keep chilled. Rewarm just enough to loosen before using. Lasagna can be assembled 1 month ahead; let cool, then cover with plastic and freeze. Let frozen lasagna thaw overnight in fridge before baking.

Editor’s note: This recipe first appeared in our February 2018 issue as part of BA’s Best, our vault of the Test Kitchen’s definitive takes on iconic dishes. It has been updated with clearer assembly instructions and guidance from additional BA Test Kitchen testing, including the option to skip parboiling regular dried lasagna noodles. #6619. Mussels With Garlicky Miso Broth

Mussels deserve your attention on weeknights. An affordable and accessible protein, they also happen to cook in less time than it takes to boil water. As the bivalves steam, they release a briny liquid, further perfuming the buttery, sake-fortified miso broth. Load up each bowl with a few good ladles, slurping every drop with an assist from crusty bread or warm rice. And why not enjoy the rest of the bottle of sake alongside your meal?

The seafood counter at your supermarket should sell rinsed and debarred mussels, but it’s easy to do at home. Discard any with cracked shells. Gently tap open raw mussels on a counter to see if they slowly close; if they do, those are okay to use. Swish them in a water-filled salad spinner or colander fitted inside a bowl, draining and refilling until water runs clear (give any especially dirty ones a scrub with a sponge). Use a towel to pull off the fibrous beard and set on a towel-lined tray in the fridge until you’re ready to cook.

More seafood dinners this way: Avgolemono Seafood Stew; Spaghetti alle Vongole; and Gorgeous Green Shrimp.

Place 2 Tbsp. scallions from 8 scallions, thinly sliced on a diagonal, in a small bowl and set aside for serving.

Melt 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large pot over medium heat. Add 8 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining scallions to pot and cook, stirring often, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. white miso paste and ½ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) and cook until miso is broken up and incorporated into butter, about 20 seconds. Pour in 1 cup dry sake or dry white wine and stir to combine, then add 3–3½ lb. mussels, scrubbed, debearded. Cover pot and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, shaking pot occasionally, until mussels open, 5–7 minutes (discard any that do not open). Remove pot from heat.

Squeeze 1 lemon half over mussels. Cut remaining 1 lemon half into wedges for serving. Taste broth and season with kosher salt if needed.

Ladle mussels and broth among shallow bowls, then scatter reserved scallions over. Serve with country-style bread or steamed white rice if desired and lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6618. Why Weed Might Actually Be Bad for Your Sleep

Everyone’s done it before. A pre-game gummy. A nighttime toke. Weed is, at this point, a widely used sleep aid. It usually works pretty well, too. But if you’ve made it a habit, you might just be sabotaging your shut-eye in the long run. According to a new October 2026 study, consuming pot in any form before bed causes people to have poorer quality of sleep—without them even realizing it. In other words: It has exactly the opposite of its intended effect. Here’s what you should know before popping an edible before you doze off.

The study, which was performed by Northwestern University researchers and published in JAMA Network, looked at 1,266 adults who participated in the Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults (CARDIA) study, which followed participants for 35 years to determine how behavioral, biological, and environmental factors affected their risk of heart disease later in life. Of that sample size, 891 wore wrist-based activity monitors for at least a week so that researchers could examine their sleep patterns. After analyzing the data, the researchers found that those who were long-term cannabis users had “poorer objective sleep, including lower sleep efficiency, greater fragmentation, and more time awake during the night,” Dr. Thanh-Huyen Vu, an author of the study and a research associate professor of preventive medicine at Northwestern University’s Feinberg School of Medicine, tells GQ.

Here’s what all of that means: Sleep efficiency is essentially how much of the time you spend in bed you’re actually asleep. So, lower sleep efficiency means spending more time lying awake instead of sleeping while sleep fragmentation refers to how often your sleep is interrupted, like when you’re unknowingly tossing and turning to get comfortable. The researchers also looked at how much total time participants spent awake during the night. It all boils down to the fact that long-term cannabis users weren’t sleeping as soundly or as continuously throughout the night—sometimes without them even knowing it.

The researchers can’t say for certain. Because the study was observational, it only established an association between long-term cannabis exposure and poorer sleep quality.

One possibility, Vu suggests, is that cannabis may “alter normal sleep architecture,” potentially changing the way the body cycles through different sleep stages.

Over time, it’s those changes that can contribute to more nighttime awakenings, which result in less restorative sleep. She says more research is needed to understand the underlying biological mechanisms.

Deep sleep is one of the most important stages of sleep because it’s the phase when your body recovers physically, processes memory, and regulates the immune system. Interruptions in sleep result in less time during the deep sleep cycle, which inhibits your body from doing all the important things that help you function properly when you’re awake. The less deep sleep you get, the worse you feel in the morning. The reason why participants don’t pick up on these mid-sleep wake-ups is that they’re easy to forget. “Sleep trackers can capture some of these patterns, even when people don’t perceive their sleep as being particularly poor,” Vu says. It’s the same way in which you think you slept eight hours one night but woke up feeling groggy regardless.

Not necessarily. Given the sample population—middle-aged adults—the results may not apply to people in other age ranges or even those who use cannabis for medical reasons. Still, Vu says it’s important for people to understand that cannabis’s relationship with sleep may be more complicated than simply helping you drift off faster.

If you regularly use cannabis before bed, paying attention to your sleep patterns may help you better understand how it’s affecting you. Wearable sleep trackers can offer some insight into nighttime awakenings and sleep efficiency, but you won’t get the same sleep analysis if you were part of a study like this. It might be worth trying out a period where you don’t use weed to fall asleep to see if it makes a difference in whether you feel more well-rested, or your mind feels sharper. Though the study still leaves a lot of questions to be answered, its data is clear enough to make anyone with a nightly gummy habit reconsider.

#6615. Butternut Pasta With Sausage and Dates

Squash and sausage are a heroic autumnal pairing, especially in a weeknight-friendly pasta. Butternut is the easiest squash to source—not to mention easily found peeled and chopped (a blessing for those with more timid knife skills). But other winter squash like acorn or red kuri can stand in as desired. Whichever squash you select, a sharp, heavy chef’s knife is best for breaking down the chunky veg. But to make your life easier, microwave the squash for 1 to 2 minutes. It will slightly soften, making it simpler—and safer—to slice through.

Rigatoni’s ribbed surface and large holes help chunky squash sauce cling and bites of seared sausage and date wedge—opting for a nutty whole wheat variety will only add to this meal’s autumnal earthiness.

More cozy pastas this way: Balsamic Mushroom and Sausage Pasta; Creamy Red Curry Pasta; and Baked Feta Pasta With Green Sauce.

Cook 1 medium butternut squash (1½–2 lb.), peeled, halved, seeds removed, cut into 1" pieces (about 6 cups), in a large pot of boiling salted water until very tender, 12–14 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer squash to a medium bowl. Reduce heat to low, cover pot, and leave on burner to keep warm.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium Dutch oven over medium-high. Add 1 lb. hot or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and break up into small pieces with a wooden spoon. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, about 3 minutes. Continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until browned all over and just cooked through, 3–4 minutes more. Transfer to a plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to medium-low. Cook 3½ oz. Medjool dates (about 6), pitted, sliced lengthwise ¾" thick, in same pan, turning halfway though, until deeply browned, 3–4 minutes. Transfer to plate with sausage; season with salt.

Add remaining 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil to pan. Add 6 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and reserved squash. Cook, scraping up browned bits and smashing squash with spoon to break up, until lightly browned and broken up into a chunky paste (pieces do not need to be even), about 5 minutes.

Meanwhile, return cooking liquid in reserved pot to a boil over high heat. Cook 12 oz. short tube pasta (such as rigatoni) until very al dente, about 3 minutes less than package directions (it will finish cooking in sauce). Drain, reserving 3 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid to squash and break up squash with spoon until a saucy consistency. Add pasta, another 1 cup pasta cooking liquid, and reserved sausage and dates. Increase heat to medium-high; cook, adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is al dente and coated in sauce, 2–3 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. sherry vinegar or balsamic vinegar. Taste pasta and add more vinegar, salt and/or pepper if needed.

#6614. Should You Worry About That Bump on Your Chest?

If you’re like most guys, you probably have plenty of little bumps and lumps on your skin. There’s the callus on your toe from training for that 10K, the razor bumps along your neck from this morning’s shave, and the skin tag on your underarm you keep meaning to get removed. While it’s often completely fine to ignore these bumps, that isn’t always the case. Some can be a red flag worth paying attention to—especially if they’re on your chest.

While male breast cancer is rare, estimates suggest that more than 2,600 men are diagnosed with an invasive form of the disease each year in the United States, and more than 500 die, according to the American Cancer Society. And one of its telltale signs is a firm bump under or near your nipple. Below, find out more about what a breast-cancer lump may look like and four other things that could be to blame for a new bump on your chest.

There isn’t a universal description of what breast cancer lumps look like in men, but there are some common characteristics to keep in mind. “Breast cancer in men typically presents as a painless, firm, or hard lump,” says Jose Pablo Leone, MD, the director of the Program for Breast Cancer in Men at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in Boston.

Another sign that the bump could be breast cancer is if it’s behind or very close to the nipple and areola. “Men have much less developed breast glandular tissue than women, which is why breast cancer in men most commonly develops near or behind the nipple,” says Dr. Leone. As for size even a lump as small as a pea can be cancerous, but by the time men go to the doctor, tumors are often larger than a marble, according to Dr. Leone. “In part because of the lack of awareness and screening, most men present with larger tumors,” he says. “But any size is worth mentioning to your doctor. Not all breast cancers feel the same, so any new or persistent breast lump should be evaluated by a healthcare professional.”

Your chest has a lot of oil glands, which can set the stage for pimples. “Staying in a sweaty shirt after a workout can make chest acne flare, especially if the fabric is tight and rubs against your skin,” says Elizabeth Bahar Houshmand, MD, a board-certified dermatologist based in Dallas. While blackheads and whiteheads are typically small and easy to identify, inflamed pimples or nodules may seem more alarming because they can be hard, painful, and form deep under the skin. When it comes to nodular acne specifically, you can’t treat it on your own. If that’s what you think you’re dealing with, see a dermatologist, who can prescribe an oral or topical medication to help clear it up.

“This is a collection of fat that forms under the skin,” says Sonya Kenkare, MD, a board-certified dermatologist at Illinois Dermatology Institute in Hinsdale, Illinois. “It is usually soft, not painful, and you can move it around in all different directions.” You don’t need to do anything about a lipoma, but if you want to get it removed, you can talk to a doctor about it.

When hair follicles get inflamed or infected, you can end up with folliculitis. “Folliculitis often looks like small pimples or pus-filled bumps centered around a hair follicle” says Dr. Houshmand. “They may itch or feel tender.”

Blockage or damage to a hair follicle can also cause epidermal inclusion cysts. These cysts occur when dead skin cells get trapped under the surface instead of shedding. “They feel somewhat firm and often have a central little black spot,” says Dr. Kenkare. Sometimes simply applying a warm compress to the area can help a cyst heal on its own, but a doctor can also inject it with a steroid to reduce swelling, drain it, or surgically remove it.

This condition occurs when breast tissue gets enlarged in men, and it can first appear as a lump under your nipple. “It often feels like a rubbery or firm disc beneath the nipple, and it may be tender,” says Dr. Houshmand. While gynecomastia can come on as a side effect of some medications, like antibiotics or antidepressants, or diseases like thyroid disorders, sometimes there is no clear cause at all.

If you’re starting to feel like it’s difficult to tell on your own what the lump on your chest might be, you’re not wrong. That’s why it’s best to have your primary care physician look at any new, unexplained bumps and tell you whether you need imaging, like a mammogram with an ultrasound. That may sound scary, but it’s really just covering your bases. “Uncommon things are uncommon, and breast cancer in men is uncommon,” says Dr. Leone. “You shouldn’t worry excessively about male breast cancer, but you should be aware of it.”

#6611. Creamy Miso Mushroom Pasta

Mushroom fans: Bookmark this recipe immediately. It will give you everything you want when you crave a creamy mushroom pasta as soon as the crisp fall air sets in. The hardworking trio of miso, Parmesan, and touch of soy sauce delivers an umami bomb of flavor that doesn’t overwhelm, but magnifies, the best of earthy mushrooms. Coupled with luscious noodles enrobed in a creamy (but not heavy) sauce, what’s not to love?

A few helpful notes for pasta success: (1) While any pasta will work, egg-based noodles, like the fettuccine I recommend here, are the best complement to the sauce. The nests (Rummo and De Cecco are great accessible brands) cook far faster than standard straight pasta, almost as fast as fresh. (2) Don’t be afraid to season your mushrooms! Yes, I know this goes against all that we’ve learned about salting them too early in the cooking process, but just a bit of salt will get them going and releasing their water faster for eventual crisp-browned edges. Don’t be alarmed if you see a pool of water at the start of the mushroom cooking—that’s to be expected and just keep going until it evaporates. (3) Don’t forget to reserve plenty of pasta cooking liquid, which is critical to the eventual sauce’s success. I prefer transferring the al dente noodles from the pasta pot to the skillet, letting any residual water come with it (and to ensure you don’t accidentally drain away that liquid gold).

Find more fall favorite meals here: Weeknight Pumpkin Chili; Cream-ish of Mushroom Soup; Mushrooms au Poivre.

Cook 12 oz. egg-based pasta (such as fettuccine nests) in a large pot of boiling salted water, stirring occasionally, until al dente, about 1 minute less than package directions.

Meanwhile, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over high. Add 1 lb. crimini or mixed mushrooms (such as button, maitake, oyster, and/or shiitake), sliced ¼" thick or torn into bite-size pieces, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and toss to coat evenly. Spread out into an even layer and cook, undisturbed, until mushrooms are starting to release their liquid, 2–3 minutes (do not be alarmed; there will be a lot). Continue to cook, tossing occasionally, until moisture is almost completely evaporated and edges of mushrooms are starting to brown, 6–8 minutes.

Reduce heat to medium-high; add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, tossing often, until garlic is fragrant and golden, 1–2 minutes. Pour in ¾ cup dry white wine, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan with a sturdy spatula or flat-edged wooden spoon, and cook until wine is mostly evaporated (you should have about 1 Tbsp. liquid left in pan), about 4 minutes. Reduce heat to medium-low. Add 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and 2 Tbsp. white miso and stir until melted and combined. Slowly pour in ½ cup heavy cream, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan; simmer until thickened slightly, 2–3 minutes. Add 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce; season with freshly ground pepper. Taste and add more salt if needed.

Using tongs, transfer pasta to mushroom mixture and add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Increase heat to medium and bring to a simmer. Cook, tossing constantly and adding ½–1 cup more pasta cooking liquid to reach desired sauce consistency if needed, until pasta is al dente and liquid has thickened slightly, about 3 minutes.

Remove pan from heat. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup) to pasta and toss to combine. Season generously with more pepper; taste and season with more salt if needed.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan and pepper.

#6610. Sticky Miso Chicken and More Recipes We Made This Week

It’s no secret that Bon Appétit editors cook a lot for work. So it should come as no surprise that we cook a lot during our off hours too. Here are the recipes we’re whipping up this month to get dinner on the table, entertain our friends, satisfy a sweet tooth, use up leftovers, and everything in between. For even more staff favorites, click here.

My husband and I recently took our 3-year-old daughter apple picking. As expected at the tail end of the season, the only apples left were Granny Smith. A perfect apple for baking, I decided to peruse our new app to see what fit the bill and found Zaynab Issa’s Caramel Apple Snacking Cake. After scanning the instructions, it seemed like a fairly straightforward one-bowl situation—the perfect pace for my lazy Sunday. I grated the apples right into a large bowl, and mixed it with the dry and wet ingredients before baking. The cake is elevated with a quick caramel that gets drizzled on top, which makes it feel fancy. —June Kim, executive editor

Armed with a fresh trio of cumin, coriander, and turmeric from Diaspora Spice Co., I decided to make Alison Roman’s Chicken Tikka Masala. It’s a bit of a project, but the payoff is worth it. The spice-rich sauce takes 30 to 40 minutes, but let it go closer to 40 for something thick, concentrated, and luxurious. Broiling is a genius move: Set on a wire rack, the yogurt-marinated chicken gets air on all sides, so it blackens instead of steaming before being added to the sauce. To accompany the main, we made a side of Priya Krishna’s Aloo Gobi in the air fryer. It came out crispy and caramelized, at least until I coated it in the creamy sauce. —Olivia Tarantino, senior shopping editor

With a name like Just-Keeps-Getting-Better Lentil Salad, how could you go wrong? My former colleague Sarah Jampel’s rightfully beloved recipe is one of those staples I’ve made so many times, I don’t even need to look at it to double-check quantities or instructions anymore. It’s become second nature. And when I’m feeling inspired, or my pantry has seen better days, it’s pretty adaptable too. This week I whipped up a huge bowl with walnuts and cashews in place of the almonds, a blood orange standing in for the lemon, and added some lovely chicories to mingle with the kale. As always, it was crunchy and fresh, tender and filling, even three days after I whipped it up. —Kelsey Jane Youngman, senior cooking editor

I love cookbook author Samantha Seneviratne’s recipes and her recent one for a tahini cake crusted with sesame seeds called to me. Just the thing for a fall weekend. I scaled down the recipe for my 8x8" pan using Kendra Vaculin’s handy conversion guide. And I did a mix of white and black sesame seeds on top for fun. It was plush and not too sweet—great for dessert and even better for breakfast the next day. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director

I’ve been holding on to this recipe for years, and it’s finally time I release it into the world. Be free Sticky Miso Chicken! It’s made with a three-ingredient marinade with stuff you probably already have in your cupboard. Equal parts miso and honey, plus a healthy splash of soy sauce mixed together creates a million-dollar burnished glaze. I slather the marinade onto chicken thighs, but you could also do chicken breast, salmon, shrimp, tofu. Go wild. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking

Every fall I stuff my pantry with cans of pumpkin purée. And fortunately our annual Pumpkin Week tells me exactly what to do with the haul. I’m always in search of more savory uses for the ingredient, and my coworker Jesse Szewczyk’s Pumpkin Black Bean Enchiladas were right up my alley. I did a mix of black and kidney beans (what was around) and I toned down the spice for my toddler who—the universe laughs—refused to eat them anyway, instead opting to smear the sauce all over his clothes. C’est la vie! —Emma Laperruque, cooking director

There is a new vendor at my greenmarket who makes incredible buffalo milk yogurt. My favorite is flavored with tangy, floral passion fruit. It’s not too sweet and works beautifully with fruit and granola. To showcase its power as a sauce, I made David Tamarkin’s apple olive oil cake (baked in an 8" round instead of a loaf) and served the yogurt underneath. For the cake, you shred a couple of apples then squeeze out their juices, which you can then drink for a baker’s treat. —Joe Sevier, senior editor, SEO & cooking

One of my favorite things is to use a banana bread recipe to make muffins and call it meal prep. I pack this gluten-free batter into tins, sprinkle on some flaxseed and pecans, and reduce the bake time. They can easily pass for breakfast, an afternoon snack, or dessert, and the recipe yields enough muffins to be enjoyed throughout the week with a scoop of yogurt or swipe of nut butter. —Kate Kassin, editorial operations manager

With a recipe entitled Bob’s Chicken and Cabbage Salad, I’m sure you’re wondering: Who the heck is Bob? Author Melissa Broder’s late father, who happened to be fervently devoted to purple cabbage. Well, Bob, me too—especially after trying this one. Per the instructions, I chopped up half a head of cabbage, baby bok choy, scallions, bean sprouts, and water chestnuts, then tossed the roughage with pulled chicken. This time around, I did cheat with a store-bought rotisserie bird to jump-start cooking (it was 8 p.m. when I started, okay?). That also meant halving the heavenly soy-ginger dressing, since I no longer needed some of it for the marinade. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking

My Test Kitchen buddy Rebecca Firkser has a wild little pasta up her sleeve that I can’t get enough of: Butternut Pasta With Sausage and Dates. When she first made it for the team, I was blown away. I would have never thought to throw dates into a pasta, but alas, it’s delicious. Each bite has something sweet, something creamy, a bit of crunch, and endless fun. —Jesse Szewczyk, senior Test Kitchen editor

Since my son started daycare in September, our household has been sick more than it has been healthy. So it makes sense that I have been on a chicken soup kick. I have it for lunch and dinner and drink mugfuls of stock between meals. My latest batch was my colleague Rebecca Firkser’s Toasted Orzo Chicken Soup, which has a beautifully spiced broth and lots of nourishing spinach. It may not be a cure-all, but close enough. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director

Delicata squash should be as popular as butternut. It’s far easier to cut (no hacks or hacking necessary), the thin skin is not only edible but tasty, and it’s got a sweet potato-like flesh that’s creamy and, well, sweet. I usually treat it simply (oil, salt and pepper, hot oven, done), but I treated myself to my former colleague Rachel Gurjar’s gussied-up Roasted Delicata Squash With Crispy Onions and I’m so glad I did. The squash itself takes no extra effort, but gathering up some toppings, like store-bought fried onions tossed with extra spices, juicy pomegranate seeds, and seasoned yogurt, transformed it into a dish I was proud to serve to guests. —Kelsey Jane Youngman, senior cooking editor

We have a new Friday tradition at our house: Pasta Alla Vodka and Caesar salad. Not rocket science, I know, but after a rough-and-tumble week of work and school, we are all reaching for some semblance of comfort. It is also easy enough to whip up that I can often beat the timing of our former Friday tradition, take-out pizza. The Caesar dressing is usually made in advance (I keep a batch in the fridge because my family lurves it) and the pasta of choice is usually rigatoni. It cooks in about the same amount of time as the sauce—I just love when that happens. —Hana Asbrink, deputy food editor

There’s nothing more perfect than a tuna melt. Buttery slices of sourdough or rye that leave a shine of grease on your fingers. Tuna salad mashed into tender flakes, speckled with crisp celery, onion, and herbs. A blanket of American cheese, so stretchy it’ll rival a mozzarella stick. And a mandatory pickle, to offer added tangy solace after each bite. I ate mine with salt-and-vinegar kettle chips stuffed inside because that’s how my favorite diner does it. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking

#6608. How Did This 14-Year-Old Get Sam Bankman-Fried on the Phone?

Journalists who’ve been anxious about losing their jobs to artificial intelligence would be wise to focus on a different, altogether less menacing but equally impressive threat: 14-year-old Eli Goldfine, the shoestring podcaster from Westchester County who last week conducted a 90-minute interview with Sam Bankman-Fried, who’s currently serving a 25-year sentence in federal prison for orchestrating a multi-billion-dollar cryptocurrency grift.

So how, exactly, does this precocious ninth grader with braces—and not a reporter from one of the scores of legacy publications who’d surely be gunning for access to the disgraced cryptocurrency king—score an interview so coveted? “I had written about Sam on Twitter a little bit, and it got picked up by the person who was at the time running Sam’s account,” Goldfine, who hosts a podcast about prediction markets called The Supercycle, told me earlier this week. “I think they were impressed with my knowledge of various parts of his criminal case.”

Goldfine’s classmates are impressed, too, even though he’s been on the receiving end of some gentle ribbing about his on-air ad reads. But can any of them say they got Bankman-Fried to speculate on the likelihood that AI will bring about the extinction of the human race? ("Less than 50%, more than 10%," by the way). Before school’s out for Thanksgiving break, Goldfine joined GQ to talk about his media diet, dream interview subject, and the mechanics of interviewing a man behind bars.

Eli Goldfine: Wait, just to step back here. Are you printing what I'm going to say, or is this just for you to know? It's not a video on the site, right?

Okay. So my podcast is primarily about prediction markets and other broader markets. And I got into that during the 2024 election. My dad showed me Polymarket and I thought, "Wow, this is really cool. It's people staking money on different sides of an outcome. And when you put all that price signal together, it converges on a really accurate probability of a given event happening. How could I investigate this more?" So I learned more about it and I started trading on a fake-money version of Polymarket.

It's called Manifold Markets. And what's cool about that one is, anyone can create their own question rather than the platform deciding. And anyway, I got really into it and then I was like, “I'll write a couple articles about this because I have some ideas.” And then I started doing interviews and it all kind of came out from that.

I think sports betting, like FanDuel and DraftKings—this stuff obviously serves very little utility because it's just the company offering these bets to the gamblers and there's no really accurate price signal coming out of that. So does that serve such an important function? Probably not. And it's fair to say the same about prediction markets on sports. Does anyone really need to know the outcome of a sports game that badly? I mean, probably not. I don't have anything against it per se, because people spend money for entertainment on other things. I mean, this is another way to spend your money. But it's not as valuable as prediction markets in some other categories. Right?

I mean, I think I've just always had a motivation to learn more about what I'm interested in. So when I start learning about something, I just get it all in my head and then I can talk about it pretty competently, I guess. I wouldn't consider myself to have natural interviewing skill. I just think I know a lot about the things that I'm interested in.

So for news, mostly Bloomberg. For social media, mostly Twitter. And then I also read articles on Substack.

So I think I had written about Sam on Twitter a little bit, and it got picked up by the person who was at the time running Sam's Twitter account. And they said, "I run this Twitter account now, but I think you have some smart ideas about Sam. Would you be interested in taking over the Twitter account?" And I was like, "Oh, yeah, that could be fun." And my dad was like, "No, you can't do that. I don't want to get sued or anything." So we ended up talking to Sam's parents about it, and they were disappointed that I wouldn't be able to take over the Twitter account. But as an alternative, they proposed, "You should just interview Sam for your podcast." So I just thought, "Wow, that's a great idea. Let's do that."

Oh, I don't know. I think they were impressed with my knowledge of various parts of his criminal case, which we actually didn't cover very much during our podcast together, since it's already been widely covered. But, yeah, I think I just had learned a lot about the case and they were like, "Well, maybe we want someone who knows a lot about the case to be able to take over his Twitter."

I don't know. I might want to skip that one for legal reasons.

I mean, I've watched so many of his other interviews, both when he was behind bars and before that, and I feel like he talks the same way to everyone. So I'm 14, you would expect maybe the average person is going to talk a little bit differently to a 14-year-old interviewer. But for him, I think it was pretty much the same, which is kind of what I expected. He's very consistent when he's talking to different people.

So when he picked up and was like, "Hi, it's Sam," I was like, "Wow, I've heard him say this in so many other interviews, but he's talking to me. That's crazy." He also called 15 minutes before the scheduled time, so I was panicking a little bit trying to get all my questions in order and deciding what order I was going to ask them in. I mean, it was pretty intense. And also, it was split up over two days in three hour windows during each day, since he can only call for 15 minutes at a time. So that was a little bit stressful.

I mean, it's mostly what I expected. He just hadn't really gone on the record about it specifically, which is why I wanted to ask him. I think his views are pretty common. He's a part of the effective altruism community. So I wasn't so surprised when he said he thought there was a 25% chance of AI destroying humanity. Obviously, if it's the average person, that might seem a little surprising. But knowing him, I wasn't very surprised.

I think there's going to be a lot of benefit in the short term, especially when we're seeing the rate of technological progress. Just in the past few months, AI has solved multiple millennium problems, which has been a huge deal. So I think there's definitely potential of AI curing diseases over the short term. But in the long term, you have to consider that there's a few examples of less intelligent things controlling more intelligent things, and that's kind of the whole point that the doomers are trying to make. Just that, when humans were smarter than the next smartest animal, we’re the ones who dominated, right?

At the end of the interview, I asked him what I call the coin flip question. "Would you take a 51-49 bet of doubling the world or destroying it?" And I asked him, "Would you take a 51-49 bet of being free tomorrow or doubling your prison time?" So I mean, there's a couple other interesting questions there I would've loved to get his take on.

Yeah. I mean, there's something funny that happened. Someone at my school walked up to me and they were like, "Hey, are you the kid who ..." Actually, wait. I actually don't want to go there.

But they were all excited. They thought it was pretty funny, and then they were impressed that it got as many views as it did. I think right now it's at about 1.3 million views, probably closer to 1.4 across all platforms. But, yeah, I think everyone was very surprised that it was able to do that well. And mostly people just think it's funny. Some responses that have been less good were people focusing on the ad read I did during the episode and mistaking it for a sportsbook, even though it's actually a free-to-play forecasting competition. So that's been the less good side of things.

Ninth grade. And I live in Westchester County, New York.

It's a good question. Maybe Marc Andreessen, in the short term.

Yeah. I'm involved a little bit with the new media team at his company, and so that would be pretty cool.

#6607. Cider-Braised Sausage and Lentils

I haven’t made a meal in the French countryside in fall; but sometimes I dream, and these slow-cooked lentils are what I’d make in such a situation. Back in my American reality, it still makes an excellent dinner or hearty weekend lunch. Look for mild smoked Austrian or German sausages, which lean on mellow herbs and warm spices (sometimes, if you’re lucky, they’re also stuffed with a nutty cheese)—this style is already cooked to a safe temperature, but the casing’s texture is greatly improved when seared before reheating. If your shop only carries sweet Italian sausage or something like an apple-stuffed chicken sausage, both work in a pinch. What a treat it will be to actually finish off that gallon of apple cider you impulsively bought last week in the lentil-braising liquid.

More great fall recipes this way: Charred Cabbage With Sausages and Apples; Pork Chops With Green Chiles and Apples; Mustardy Cider-Braised Pork Chops.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 6–8 smoked Austrian or German sausages (1–1½ lb.), turning often, until deeply browned on all sides, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a plate.

Combine 1 large red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 3 celery stalks, finely chopped, 1 large carrot, peeled, finely chopped, 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in same pan. Reduce heat to medium and cook, stirring often and scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan, until vegetables are softened, 6–8 minutes. Add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and cook, stirring, just until fragrant, about 1 minute.

Add 2 cups low-sodium chicken or vegetable broth, 1½ cups apple cider, 1½ cups French green lentils, picked through, rinsed, ½ cup finely chopped parsley, 3 Tbsp. Dijon or whole grain mustard, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt to pan. Increase heat to high and bring to a boil. Cook until liquid is slightly reduced, about 5 minutes. Cover pan, reduce heat to medium-low, and cook until lentils are tender and most of the liquid is absorbed but mixture is still saucy, 30–35 minutes.

Uncover pan and stir in 1 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar or red wine vinegar. Nestle sausages into lentil mixture and add any juices pooled on plate. Simmer until sausages are warmed through, about 5 minutes. Top with parsley leaves and reserved celery leaves to serve.

#6606. Brave New Visions Creativity as Rebellion

PhotoVogue is proud to unveil the shortlist of 100 photographers and video makers selected for Brave New Visions: Creativity as Rebellion, our Global Open Call dedicated to the power of creativity to challenge the status quo, question established narratives, and imagine alternative futures. With 95,758 submissions from 9,160 artists across 155 regions, the response to this year's Open Call was extraordinary. But beyond the numbers, what moved us most was the imagination, urgency, and creative courage of the work we received. We live in a world saturated with images. More images are produced and consumed than ever before, yet more images do not necessarily mean more understanding, more imagination, or more freedom. What matters is not simply creating something new, but finding a way to make us see, feel, or question something we might otherwise have overlooked. Perhaps today, one of the most rebellious things an artist can do is refuse to give us another image we already know. Rebellion does not always announce itself loudly. It can be political and confrontational, but it can also be intimate, poetic, playful, uncomfortable, or deeply personal. It can take the form of tenderness, humor, beauty, or an unexpected way of looking at something familiar. What makes it rebellious is the freedom to question what we have been taught to accept and to imagine what might exist beyond it. This year's Open Call brought together an extraordinary range of ideas, emotions, and visual languages. Some works confront urgent social and political realities. Others explore identity, memory, belonging, desire, or the complexities of human experience. What connects the 100 selected artists is not a shared aesthetic or a single definition of rebellion, but a willingness to take risks, experiment, and follow their own vision. Images do more than represent the world. They influence how we understand it, whose stories we recognize, and what we believe is possible. The artists presented here remind us that creativity can do more than reflect reality. It can challenge the assumptions through which we see it and make space for futures we have not yet imagined.

What's Next This shortlist marks the beginning of the next chapter of Brave New Visions: Creativity as Rebellion. In the coming weeks, we will announce which artists from the shortlist have been selected to exhibit at the next edition of the PhotoVogue Festival, as well as the three artists who will receive the PhotoVogue Grants. We will also reveal the festival's dates and location. We invite you to return to this page and follow PhotoVogue on Instagram for these announcements. Above all, we want to thank every artist who trusted us with their work. Selecting 100 artists from such an extraordinary response was incredibly difficult. This shortlist represents only a fraction of the talent, imagination, and creative courage we encountered. The future is not something we simply inherit. It is something we have the power to imagine.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Farīsāt – Gunpowder’s Daughters’. For centuries, tbourida, the Moroccan equestrian tradition reenacting ancient Arab military manoeuvres, was an exclusively male domain. Today, women are mounting their horses, leading their own troupes and rewriting the rules of a centuries-old practice. Known as farisat, these riders are challenging the patriarchal structures that have kept them out of the arena, claiming a place in Morocco’s cultural heritage. Following several all-female sorbas across the country, Pinzi documents a quiet but determined shift in tradition, where simply taking the reins can become an act of resistance.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Heaven Belongs to You’. What if divinity had never been somewhere above us, but always within us? Okoro reimagines heaven through the presence of contemporary African subjects, casting real individuals as living mythologies whose everyday existence carries the weight of the sacred. Drawing on the power of ancestral narratives, the series challenges the mythologies that have historically dictated who is entitled to embody purity, power and the divine. Here, divinity is neither inherited nor bestowed: it belongs to everyone, and begins with the self.

This photograph is part of the series ‘We Didn’t Choose to Be Born Here’. At its heart are two contrasting responses to Apartheid: while Makepe’s grandfather fled South Africa for Botswana in search of a safer life, his great-uncle became a prominent anti-Apartheid activist and political prisoner. Blending staged portraiture, documentary photography and re-enactments, Makepe brings these histories into the present, collaborating with relatives to reconstruct memories and embody those who came before them. Through this intergenerational portrait, he examines the choices we inherit, the weight of political responsibility and how personal circumstances shape our relationship with collective struggle.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Grosse’. Taking its title from a word historically associated with shame and stigma, the project turns an insult into a means of questioning the beauty standards imposed on contemporary bodies. Through staged self-portraits, fictional imagery and distorted mirrors, the artist explores the uneasy relationship between self-acceptance and the desire to conform. Drawing on her own experience with weight-loss medication, she confronts the contradictions of a culture that encourages us to love our bodies while relentlessly urging us to change them. A recurring hybrid figure, suspended between reality and imagination, embodies the internalised gaze through which the body becomes both an object of scrutiny and a site of control.

This photograph is part of the project ‘4ever &ver &ver’, an anthology of three video works and one photographic piece exploring how young people navigate a social reality where online and offline lives increasingly overlap. Drawing on digital behaviours, everyday conversations and staged situations, Jip Schalkx examines a generation shaped by visibility, self-performance and the constant possibility of being seen. In a world where even the most mundane moments become potential content, identity and connection are increasingly negotiated through the logic of social platforms. Part observation, part personal inquiry, the four interconnected works form a fragmented yet intimate portrait of the present, where reality and fiction are never quite separate.

We Need To Talk In Whispers: Case Study of Alfred

This photograph is part of the series ‘We Need to Talk in Whispers: Case Study of Alfred’. The project began with an unexpected discovery: a weathered notebook found on an overnight train in India, filled with handwritten notes, newspaper clippings and fragments of correspondence documenting lives marked by death and disappearance. Following these scattered traces, Bose travelled to Ebeltoft, Denmark, to investigate the story of Alfred, a man who lived with schizophrenia during the Second World War. Moving between archival research, oral histories, documentary photography and speculation, he reconstructs an inner world through the places, objects and silences left behind. At the intersection of memory and imagination, the work asks what whispers can reveal about the experiences society would rather leave unspoken.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Untitled’, in which Peristiani turns the domestic interior into a stage for the power dynamics that shape women's lives. A space conventionally associated with intimacy and safety becomes a setting for surveillance, control and quiet acts of rebellion. Through two recurring figures, uncomfortable poses, obstructed mirrors and carefully choreographed gestures, she explores the tension between being watched and attempting to escape the gaze. Here, even the most familiar household objects become instruments of control, while the body itself becomes a means of resistance, reclaiming space through movement and disruption.

This excerpt is part of video project ‘AFK (Away From Keyboard)’. First-person shooter games such as Counter-Strike offer players the chance to embody idealised versions of militarised masculinity, where dominance and aggression are built into the game itself. Drawing on his own teenage experience of struggling with masculinity and sexuality, van Gent revisits this familiar gaming environment through a queer lens. The installation features three looping animations using original 3D game models, whose subtle gestures and unexpected movements disrupt the hypermasculine behaviour expected of their characters. By introducing moments of vulnerability and ambiguity into a world built around military prowess, AFK asks what happens when masculinity refuses to play by the rules. Watch Full Video Here

This photograph is part of the project ‘Una Storia Italiana’. Rivas Bao revisits the story of Imane Fadil, an Italian-Moroccan model and aspiring sports journalist who became a key witness in the trial surrounding Silvio Berlusconi’s infamous ‘Bunga Bunga’ parties. After testifying about the exploitation of young women at his private residence, Fadil died in suspicious circumstances in 2019, aged just 34. Combining archival material, photographs taken inside Fadil’s Milan home and AI-generated imagery, Rivas Bao reconstructs the images that were described in court but never visually documented. Reclaiming the visual language of Berlusconian television and propaganda, the project assembles a counter-narrative from the fragments of a national memory still reluctant to confront its own Me Too moment.

This photograph is part of the series ‘The Stars That Don’t Look Back’. Drawing on intimate memories shared by three generations of women in Taiwan, Chen weaves together family photographs, historical archives and literature to explore how women's lives are shaped by the forces of history. Against the backdrop of Japanese colonial rule and the White Terror, the project examines how women were represented, remembered and often silenced, from restrictions on personal appearance to the private narratives preserved in family albums. Moving between the political and the deeply personal, Chen traces the quiet resilience passed down through generations, finding in women's shared memories a fragile but enduring sense of belonging and inner peace.

This photograph is part of the series ‘CLICHES’. Growing up in Morocco means inheriting a wealth of stories, sayings, stereotypes and beliefs that shape how we see ourselves and the world around us. Through staged photography blending documentary references, symbolism, fashion and fiction, Nassereddine Anjar revisits these familiar narratives, transforming them into images that sit between recognition and questioning. Approaching them as a living archive of shared memory, he explores the tensions between tradition and modernity, myth and everyday life, and the contradictions of a generation negotiating its relationship with heritage.

This photograph is part of the series ‘We Too Have Wings’. Growing up between places, Hajo returns to memories of his grandmother’s house outside Khartoum, where he watched pigeons take flight and find their way home. Having witnessed both the revolution and the war in Sudan before leaving once again, he now reflects on displacement from Doha, where the project was made. Through images of family, places and everyday life, he explores whether home is somewhere we return to, or something we learn to carry and rebuild within ourselves.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Brewed Reflections: The Poetry of Ataya’. Introduced to Salam by his uncle during childhood, Ataya, a West African tea ritual, becomes a way to reconnect with personal roots and a wider sense of belonging. Beyond the preparation and sharing of tea, these gatherings create space for conversation, debate, laughter and simply being together. In a world increasingly shaped by digital connection and individualism, Salam sees this collective ritual as a quiet form of resistance, celebrating the value of physical presence and the bonds that emerge when people take the time to gather.

If life is a video game, the graphics are great, but the plot is confusing and the tutorial is way too long.

This photograph is part of the series ‘If life is a video game, the graphics are great, but the plot is confusing and the tutorial is way too long'. Taking Elon Musk as both subject and symbol of our age, Cedric Zellweger examines the contradictions of hyper-consumption, technological utopianism and the fantasies of global elites. Through elaborate still lifes staged with hundreds of objects and photographed on large-format analogue film, he assembles a surreal visual commentary on contemporary politics and late-stage capitalism. Part satire, part dystopian spectacle, the project draws on everything from space exploration to meme culture to ask who gets to shape our collective future, and whether it is one we actually want.

This photograph is part of the series ‘TRANSFER’. For twenty years, Tan lived in their parents’ apartment while keeping their queer identity invisible. Now, they revisit the space as both a home and a departure lounge, a place to which they remain tied but from which they have long felt the need to escape. Through self-portraiture, the apartment becomes an imagined airport transfer station, suspended between belonging and elsewhere. In Chinese, zhuǎnjī (转机) means both “transfer” and “chance”: a small linguistic coincidence that captures the possibility of departure, transformation and a different beginning.

This photograph is part of the series ‘The Sake of Our Resistance’. Through portraits of family, friends and collaborators in Togo and its diaspora, Delali Ayivi explores resistance as an everyday practice rooted in community, creativity and mutual care. Beginning with a familiar story of an orange shared among an entire family, the project traces a belief in collective resources and responsibility across generations. Women’s organisations, village initiatives and the work of hairdressers, designers and sculptors become expressions of a quiet persistence. Accompanied by reflections from ten Togolese voices, the series asks what resistance can look like when protest is not always possible, and how simply sustaining one another can become an act of defiance.

This excerpt is part of the multimedia project ‘Genesis, We Were Trying to Build a Home’. Drawing on her experience of growing up in the foster system, Mikhailia Petersen explores displacement as both a physical condition and something carried within the body. Through self-portraiture, performance and ritual, she returns to her relationship with her mother, inherited wounds and the histories of land and belonging in Cape Town. Menstrual blood, flowers, fire and water become materials for mourning and renewal, as Petersen confronts the legacies of colonialism, apartheid and intergenerational trauma. Rather than seeking to erase the past, the work asks how a sense of home might be rebuilt from what remains. Watch Full Video Here

This excerpt is part of the multimedia project Praxis Modulus, by Ayomide Tejuoso aka Plantation. Spanning photography, film, installation and performance, the work constructs a contemporary Black mythology through the visual languages of Ifá, fashion imagery and African American aesthetic philosophies. Blue recurs throughout as a symbol of death, sacredness and liminality, shaping a world populated by self-portraits and portraits of other Black figures. Drawing on the visual practices of Fred Moten and Arthur Jafa, Tejuoso develops an unsettling visual universe where beauty, ritual and decadence converge, confronting the violence of necro-capitalism through acts of image-making and resistance.

This photograph is part of the series ‘Of Animals and Us’. Over the past four years, Irina Werning has visited agricultural fairs and livestock shows in Argentina and the UK, searching for moments when people and animals seem to mirror one another. Groomed, judged and admired, they become unlikely participants in what the photographer describes as a Darwinian theatre of look-alikes. Behind the humour lies a more uneasy reflection on our relationship with animals: some share our homes and daily lives, while others remain out of sight until they reach our plates. Through images that invite a second look, Werning explores the growing distance between humans, animals and the landscapes they once shared.

This photograph is part of the photographic project ‘Muñecas & Muñequerxs’. In its first chapter, set in Guanajuato, Mexico, Silvana Trevale explores the tradition of cartonería, the art of transforming paper and paste into figures used in play, ritual, satire and devotion. Working alongside local artisans, she documents the knowledge passed down through generations while reinterpreting familiar customs through contemporary questions of identity, gender and race. From the ceremonial destruction of Judas figures to the reinvention of a quinceañera ritual through a trans woman, the project reveals how traditions can become spaces of both preservation and resistance, continually reshaped by those who keep them alive.

This photograph is part of the ongoing series ‘Loose Fist’. Following a violent homophobic attack in his hometown of Kathmandu, Arhant Shrestha began photographing men as a way to confront the fear and mistrust he had developed. What started as an exercise in exposure gradually became an inquiry into masculinity, intimacy and the possibility of connection. Through portraits and staged encounters with strangers and former classmates, Shrestha revisits the codes of male friendship, aggression and tenderness that shaped his own adolescence. In proposing care as an alternative to militarised masculinity, the project traces a personal journey from isolation towards a sense of community.

This photograph is part of ‘5BFW — 5 Bocas Fashion Week’, a project by Natasha Ribas and Allan Weber that brings fashion into the streets of Rio de Janeiro’s favela of 5B, placing its residents at the centre of the story. Local men with no previous modelling experience become the faces of a campaign that challenges conventional ideas of beauty, style and who gets to occupy fashion imagery. Designer clothes meet gold chains, scapulars and personal belongings, set against the textures of everyday life. Conceived as an unprecedented event for the community, the project uses fashion as a tool for visibility, self-recognition and the reimagining of a place too often seen through the eyes of outsiders.

This photograph is part of the series ‘What If We Lived Among Gods?’. Dammy Twitch brings African deities into the everyday settings of contemporary Nigeria, imagining a world where the spiritual and the mundane exist side by side. Each image places a different god or goddess within familiar surroundings, challenging the distance that modern life has created from ancestral belief systems. Part visual theology, part cultural reclamation, the series insists that African spiritual traditions have not disappeared, but continue to shape the present. Rather than looking back with nostalgia, Twitch invites viewers to recognise the divine in ordinary life and reconsider what has been inherited, forgotten and kept alive.

This photograph is part of the series 'Hypnagogia'. Drawing on the fleeting state between wakefulness and sleep, Myles Loftin uses fashion photography to build a world where imagination takes the lead. Playful styling and dreamlike imagery explore the shifting boundaries between consciousness and the unconscious, softness and masculinity, fantasy and reality. With a sense of childlike wonder, the series embraces the strange freedom of the hypnagogic state, creating space for dreaming in a world that increasingly leaves little room for it.

good girls go to heaven, bad girls go wandering

This excerpt is part of the multimedia project ‘good girls go to heaven, bad girls go wandering’. Developed in collaboration with poet and artist Ranu Ritamalan through fieldwork across Indonesia, Brandon Lopez’s project follows lives lived outside the expected milestones of family, marriage and belonging. Moving between photography, speculative essays, poetry and string figures, the work questions how social structures shape our sense of time, direction and purpose. Its subjects include a monkey navigating Jakarta’s formal economy and a traffic officer observed through the rhythms of a single intersection. Here, wandering becomes a form of refusal: a way to imagine what might emerge beyond the destinations society sets for us.

This photograph is part of the ongoing series ‘New Order’. From the perspective of a young adult raised on pacifist and diplomatic ideals, Louis Roth documents Europe’s shifting relationship with militarisation amid a new arms race. Combining NATO exercises, military parades and official events with quieter scenes of everyday life, the project observes how military and civilian worlds increasingly overlap. Beginning in the Baltic states and expanding across Europe, Roth explores the ambivalence surrounding this transformation, known in Germany as Zeitenwende. His restrained visual language resists military spectacle, using photography to question how a new political reality gradually becomes part of everyday life.

This photograph is part of the ongoing series ‘NORA’. Photographing her sixty-year-old friend, Bettina Pittaluga explores ageing as a process of continual transformation rather than disappearance. Through playful, intimate portrait sessions, the two revisit the many faces Nora has inhabited and those still to come. Against a visual culture increasingly devoted to smoothing wrinkles, erasing grey hair and concealing the passage of time, the project embraces the body's capacity for change, desire and reinvention. Made together as they grow older, the series remains open-ended, allowing identity to shift with every encounter.

This photograph is part of the ongoing series ‘The Garden’. Made between 2020 and 2026, Ville Varumo’s work traces the unsettled feeling of living between a former home and a new city, caught between the desire to escape and the longing to put down roots. Through quiet observations of streets, strangers, nocturnal facades, a recurring white dog and, eventually, the artist’s newborn, seemingly unrelated moments begin to form a personal visual diary. Moving between public and private spaces, the photographs find the extraordinary in the everyday, reflecting on home as something continually built, lost and reimagined.

This excerpt is part of the multimedia project ‘No Man’s Wedding’. Through a twisted, symbolic wonderland, Carolina Dutca and Valentin Sidorenko explore the experience of war using the archetypes and rituals of folk narratives. Their story follows a man going to war as a groom approaches his wedding, descending into an underworld where he attempts to outwit death. Shells, soil and baptismal imagery become ambiguous symbols of passage, faith and mortality. Rather than documenting conflict directly, the artists draw on the language of fairy tales to examine the existential questions that war leaves in its wake.

This excerpt is part of the multimedia project ‘...The Candle Whispered Them Here’. Through analogue and tintype photography and photographic sculpture, Delali Cofie imagines an archive for Ghanaian folklore, giving stories a physical place to endure. Five figures from Ghanaian history and mythology, including Anansi, Yaa Asantewaa and Okomfo Anokye, find refuge in everyday household objects, transformed into vessels for collective memory. Blending the intimacy of oral storytelling with the permanence of photographic objects, Cofie reflects on what happens to stories as they fade from memory, and how the rituals of sharing them might keep them alive.

This excerpt is part of the video project ‘Fireworks on the Swamp’. Begun in 2013 and completed in 2020, Sergei Prokofiev’s work emerged from a period of political disillusionment and growing social tension in Russia. Conceived as an attempt to make art outside the expectations of the market and institutional system, the project uses pyrotechnics in a desolate, swamp-like landscape to evoke an atmosphere of hostility and uncertainty. Developed over seven years, it reflects on the limits of artistic interpretation and the possibility of experiencing reality directly, before it settles into a coherent narrative. Watch Full Video Here

This excerpt is part of the multimedia project ‘The Boat’. Over two years, Stein Henningsen pushed an old traditional wooden boat through winter landscapes, rowed it across open water and drift ice, and eventually set it alight in front of a glacier. Bringing fire and ice into direct confrontation, the performance turns the boat into a striking image of our relationship with the natural world. Part of Henningsen’s ongoing exploration of elemental forces, the work confronts the paralysis that often accompanies awareness of the environmental crisis, inviting viewers to experience the fragile balance between human life and the forces of nature. Watch Full Video Here

This photograph is part of Elizabeth Haust’s "All About Loneliness", an evolving collection of images connected by an interest in magic, ritual, solitude and the body. Moving between self-observation and fiction, Haust treats photography as a way to give shape to experiences that resist straightforward expression. Ordinary spaces become stages for private ceremonies, while gestures and objects take on symbolic meaning. Together, the images form an intimate emotional archive, exploring vulnerability, desire, isolation and the invisible systems of belief we build to make sense of being alive.

This excerpt is part of the film ‘STARE’. Created by Bijoy Shetty in collaboration with designer Bhavya Ramesh for Bhavya Ramesh Jewellery and NorBlack NorWhite, the work explores the female form beyond the limits of expectation. Moving between softness and rage, vulnerability and strength, the film embraces femininity in its extremes, drawing on the mystical as a space for release and self-acceptance. Watch Full Video Here

This photograph is part of the series ‘The Holy Mountains’. Bringing together the mountains of Mexico’s Chiapas highlands and the Swiss Alps, Diego Moreno creates a fictional landscape where two seemingly distant cultural worlds become mirrors of one another. Through photography, collage and graphic intervention, he draws on ancestral myths, folk tales and religious traditions to explore the ways identity is shaped by territory, colonisation and cultural mixing. The result is a personal mythology in which folklore becomes a way to revisit inherited histories and imagine new ones.

This photograph is part of the ongoing project ‘Everything I Want to Tell You’. Through a weekly exchange of images, videos and shared fantasies, Sadie Cook and Jo Pawlowska trace the ways class, illness, migration, gender and sexuality leave their marks on the body and everyday life. Moving between personal archives and staged scenes, their collaboration builds an ever-expanding visual world where memory and desire blur. Presented through large-scale installations of thousands of images, the work captures identity as something continually unsettled, taken apart and reassembled.

This photograph is part of the ongoing series ‘A bit more yellow, a bit more sour...’. Through portraits of friends and family, Eszter Sárkány explores the complicated relationship younger generations have with Hungarian traditions, caught between the desire to reconnect with their cultural roots and the need to distance themselves from their political appropriation. Rather than turning away from the past, she looks for ways to reinterpret it, finding in familiar rituals and symbols room for personal expression, autonomy and new forms of belonging. As Hungary enters a period of political transition, the series shifts from anger towards a more open-ended reflection on what might come next.

This photograph is part of the prokect "Please pierce your bones into mine", dedicated to the artist’s great-aunt, Jacoba Manders. Despite a 71-year age difference, the two shared a bond that felt more like friendship than family, becoming a way for the artist to reflect on ageing, intimacy and the experience of saying goodbye. Through images that hold both Jacoba’s history and the artist’s imagined future, the work considers what passes between generations beyond material inheritance. What remains is an emotional legacy of tenderness, resilience and truth, quietly shaping the lives of those who carry it forward.

This excerpt is part of the video installation ‘Afterparty’. In a vast desert landscape, fifty figures repeat familiar routines: gambling, scrolling, digging holes, burning books, practising yoga. Gabriel Barcia-Colombo imagines a world after collapse in which the spectacle may be over, but everyday life carries on as if nothing has happened. Structured around three pillars of contemporary life, knowledge, connection and leisure, the triptych examines our growing dependence on technology and the systems that shape what we know and believe. In its final moments, the figures turn towards the viewer, extending an invitation to join the party, or recognise we never really left. Watch Full Video Here

This photograph is part of the ongoing series ‘Touch’. Drawing on Alexis Kleshik’s own experience of sex work and queer life, the series explores the relationships that take shape between friends, lovers, clients, coworkers and chosen family.
